# Rediscovery Of African Burial Grounds Provides Chance For Healing

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HBxfqOYWdZY)

(ANALYSIS) In the course of construction work in 2013, the remains of [36 individuals of African descent were uncovered](https://www.augustachronicle.com/story/news/2013/02/23/dozens-unmarked-graves-thought-date-18th-century-discovered-charleston/14463656007/) in the heart of downtown Charleston, South Carolina. They had lain hidden for some 200 years in an unmarked 18th-century burial ground.

For more than two centuries, such burial grounds, especially those in the former American slave states, have often been erased or obscured — paved over by parking lots, built upon by highways or private development, or simply left unknown and untended. In recent years, descendant communities in places such as [Bethesda, Maryland](https://bethesdamagazine.com/2024/09/05/state-supreme-court-rules-black-cemetery-remains-likely-interred-under-bethesda-apartments/), [Richmond, Virginia](https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2024/07/05/richmond-virginia-shockoe-african-cemetery/), [St. Petersburg, Florida](https://www.abcactionnews.com/news/local-news/archived-reports-reveal-african-american-cemeteries-erased-in-st-petersburg), and [Sugarland, Texas](https://www.npr.org/2023/06/18/1183018493/a-cemetery-in-sugar-land-texas-forces-city-to-confront-its-history), have called for greater recognition and respect for these long-neglected sites.

As a [public archaeologist and educator](https://charleston.edu/sociology-anthropology/faculty/gilmore-joanna.php) who has spent over a decade working in Charleston, South Carolina, I co-direct the [Anson Street African Burial Ground project](https://www.asabgproject.com/) – the community-led effort to honor and respectfully lay to rest the 36 African ancestors whose remains were uncovered in 2013.

This Charleston project reflects a [growing recognition of African American burial grounds](https://blackcemeterynetwork.org/new-page) as [important historical memory sites](https://www.sapiens.org/archaeology/african-american-cemeteries-destruction/) and unique sources of genealogical information. Yet there is still [limited public understanding](https://www.aaihs.org/unmarked-and-unburied-the-unsettling-of-black-death/) about how engaging with these places of sacred rest can promote collective healing, reconciliation and cross-cultural understanding.

## **Cemeteries obscured by history**

Since the British colonial period, racist laws and customs across America prevented enslaved and free people of African descent from using white burial grounds to bury their dead. On plantations, [enslavers controlled where and how the enslaved were buried](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315419053) and whether burials could be marked or visited. In cities from Charleston to New York, [segregated burial grounds](https://www.ccpl.org/charleston-time-machine/forgotten-dead-charlestons-public-cemeteries-1672-1794), many now forgotten, were established by local authorities for indigent Black and white people.

Pushed to the margins, people of African descent maintained burial traditions and used impermanent or specific grave markers such as shells, bottles, clocks or ceramics — [items that were culturally meaningful](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03374216) but often invisible or unimportant to white observers. As a result, many of these sites were neither recorded in historical documents nor officially recognized as burial grounds.

From the 1770s, [African American churches](https://savingplaces.org/stories/first-baptist-church-williamsburg), [benevolent societies and funeral homes](https://www.uapress.com/product/black-charlestonians/) sought to establish cemeteries where Black communities could honor the dead with dignity. What began regionally — especially in Charleston and Philadelphia – quickly spread nationally during the 19th century across the American South and North.

In the decades after Reconstruction, and especially during the Jim Crow era, nearly [6 million African Americans moved north and west](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/long-lasting-legacy-great-migration-180960118/) to escape racial violence and seek better opportunities – an event known as the Great Migration. This movement often [severed ties between families](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/190696/the-warmth-of-other-suns-by-isabel-wilkerson/) and ancestral burial grounds in the South. As churches and burial societies lost members, many cemeteries fell into disrepair and were [officially labeled “abandoned” by local authorities or developers](https://charlestoncitypaper.com/2008/07/02/hidden-heritage/).

In both rural and urban areas, Black burial grounds were often located on less valuable lands, sites that today are increasingly threatened by gentrification, development and the effects of [climate change](https://yaleclimateconnections.org/2022/11/historic-black-cemeteries-threatened-by-extreme-weather/).

The [Gullah Geechee](https://www.ugapress.org/9780820327839/the-gullah-people-and-their-african-heritage/), who descend from enslaved Africans from West Africa and still preserve unique cultural traditions in the southeastern U.S., argue [these burial sites were never abandoned and that ancestors are still present](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2021/10/04/when-black-history-is-unearthed-who-gets-to-speak-for-the-dead).

This perspective views the dead as actively connected to the living. For them, lacking formally designated cemetery space doesn’t make the sites any less sacred.

## **A tradition of sacred spaces**

For many African Americans, especially in the South, death during slavery was seen as not merely an ending but a spiritual return — a “homegoing.”

Rooted in [West African spiritual worldviews and carried through other traditions in America](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/africanatlantic-cultures-and-the-south-carolina-lowcountry/C02F984E2F2C945B9B945496EF28CE6B), the act of burial was often viewed as a release from bondage, a return to the ancestors and a step toward wholeness.

The Gullah Geechee traditions of coastal South Carolina emphasize ancestral presence, spiritual continuity and the sanctity of the land. In that worldview, with a porous boundary between the living and the dead, proper burial and remembrance are not only cultural imperatives but necessary for community well-being.

It was not until the early 1990s that recognition of rights over ancestral remains and sacred burial grounds began to find a wider audience.

Inspired by the 1990 [Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-43/subtitle-A/part-10) that recognized Indigenous rights over ancestral remains, African American communities increasingly asserted their own rights to ethical research, respectful handling and meaningful memorialization, especially during the 1991 [New York African Burial Ground](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03374233) project, which reshaped public memory and [archaeological ethics](http://www.jstor.org/stable/3069222).

Discovered during construction in lower Manhattan, the 18th-century burial ground contained the remains of more than 400 enslaved and free Africans. Community advocacy led to the site’s protection, descendant-led research, ceremonial reburial and the [establishment of a national memorial in 2006](https://www.nps.gov/afbg/index.htm).

Since this time, across the U.S. and the Atlantic world, descendant-led ceremonies from [Portsmouth, New Hampshire](https://africanburyinggroundnh.org/index.html), to [Key West, Florida](https://www.africanburialgroundathiggsbeach.org/discovery), have restored dignity to ancestral remains.

Meanwhile, efforts to [preserve African American](https://www-nature-com.nuncio.cofc.edu/articles/d41586-021-01320-4) burial grounds, [including by national scholar organizations](https://americananthro.org/about/committees-and-task-forces/tcethr/) and [federal lawmakers](https://adams.house.gov/media-center/press-releases/adams-files-amendment-fund-african-american-burial-grounds-preservation), continue amid political debates over how history should be remembered and taught.

## **What made the Anson Street project unique**

In Charleston, the Anson Street African Burial Ground project stands out for the way Gullah Geechee traditions and descendant collaboration shaped every stage of the process — from scientific study to reinterment.

Launched as a community-led initiative in 2017, the team began by listening. Through regular gatherings, they invited questions about the ancestors’ lives and identities, and about their hopes for the reburial, centering Black community voices at every stage. The team combined [scientific investigations of ancestry and health](https://doi.org/10.1002/ajpa.24149) while also creating space for spiritual guidance, ceremony and descendant leadership.

In doing so, the project became more than a study of the past; it became a communal act of repair and remembrance, [reconnecting Charleston’s present communities with the ancestors whose stories](https://doi.org/10.1017/aaq.2023.105) had long been buried.

Over the next two years, the team wove this commitment into every aspect of its work: youth art programs, a college course on memorial design, public exhibitions, and school partnerships. One of the most moving moments came from conversations with schoolchildren, who decided that the ancestors should be given names before they were reburied.

That naming ceremony took place in April 2019. The names were conferred by [Natalie Washington-Weik, a Yorùbá-Orisa Ọ̀ṣun priestess](http://hdl.handle.net/2152/ETD-UT-2009-08-309), a spiritual leader in a West African tradition and an African historian. She described the ritual as an “important step forward in reclaiming the humanity of the deceased people who were most likely forced to travel across the Atlantic Ocean under the terror of other humans – who saw them merely as animals.”

The ancestors were finally reinterred in a powerful public ceremony that reflected their ancestries and West-Central African spiritual traditions.

## **When pain is acknowledged, healing can occur**

The 2019 naming and reinterment ceremonies were not simply commemorations; they were rituals of remembrance and healing.

Construction for a [permanent memorial](https://www.asabgproject.com/a-memorial-for-the-ancestors) at the Anson Street site, designed by artist Stephen L. Hayes Jr., has now begun. At its center is a basin fabricated with sacred soil collected from 36 African-descended burial grounds across the Charleston region. From the basin, 36 bronze hands will rise – cast from living community members whose profiles reflect those of the ancestors. Raised in gestures of prayer, resistance and reverence, these hands link past to present.

Throughout the memorialization process, community members reflected on what it meant to participate in such a project. Many spoke of feeling pride, reverence, joy, sadness and peace. “This conversation makes me feel complete,” one participant said.

As Charleston demonstrates, these projects are not only about preserving the past – they are acts of recognition, respect and reconciliation, helping communities nationwide confront and honor the histories long denied to African-descended peoples.

# Rediscovery Of African Burial Grounds Provides Chance For Healing

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HBxfqOYWdZY)

(ANALYSIS) In the course of construction work in 2013, the remains of [36 individuals of African descent were uncovered](https://www.augustachronicle.com/story/news/2013/02/23/dozens-unmarked-graves-thought-date-18th-century-discovered-charleston/14463656007/) in the heart of downtown Charleston, South Carolina. They had lain hidden for some 200 years in an unmarked 18th-century burial ground.

For more than two centuries, such burial grounds, especially those in the former American slave states, have often been erased or obscured — paved over by parking lots, built upon by highways or private development, or simply left unknown and untended. In recent years, descendant communities in places such as [Bethesda, Maryland](https://bethesdamagazine.com/2024/09/05/state-supreme-court-rules-black-cemetery-remains-likely-interred-under-bethesda-apartments/), [Richmond, Virginia](https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2024/07/05/richmond-virginia-shockoe-african-cemetery/), [St. Petersburg, Florida](https://www.abcactionnews.com/news/local-news/archived-reports-reveal-african-american-cemeteries-erased-in-st-petersburg), and [Sugarland, Texas](https://www.npr.org/2023/06/18/1183018493/a-cemetery-in-sugar-land-texas-forces-city-to-confront-its-history), have called for greater recognition and respect for these long-neglected sites.

As a [public archaeologist and educator](https://charleston.edu/sociology-anthropology/faculty/gilmore-joanna.php) who has spent over a decade working in Charleston, South Carolina, I co-direct the [Anson Street African Burial Ground project](https://www.asabgproject.com/) – the community-led effort to honor and respectfully lay to rest the 36 African ancestors whose remains were uncovered in 2013.

This Charleston project reflects a [growing recognition of African American burial grounds](https://blackcemeterynetwork.org/new-page) as [important historical memory sites](https://www.sapiens.org/archaeology/african-american-cemeteries-destruction/) and unique sources of genealogical information. Yet there is still [limited public understanding](https://www.aaihs.org/unmarked-and-unburied-the-unsettling-of-black-death/) about how engaging with these places of sacred rest can promote collective healing, reconciliation and cross-cultural understanding.

## **Cemeteries obscured by history**

Since the British colonial period, racist laws and customs across America prevented enslaved and free people of African descent from using white burial grounds to bury their dead. On plantations, [enslavers controlled where and how the enslaved were buried](https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315419053) and whether burials could be marked or visited. In cities from Charleston to New York, [segregated burial grounds](https://www.ccpl.org/charleston-time-machine/forgotten-dead-charlestons-public-cemeteries-1672-1794), many now forgotten, were established by local authorities for indigent Black and white people.

Pushed to the margins, people of African descent maintained burial traditions and used impermanent or specific grave markers such as shells, bottles, clocks or ceramics — [items that were culturally meaningful](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03374216) but often invisible or unimportant to white observers. As a result, many of these sites were neither recorded in historical documents nor officially recognized as burial grounds.

From the 1770s, [African American churches](https://savingplaces.org/stories/first-baptist-church-williamsburg), [benevolent societies and funeral homes](https://www.uapress.com/product/black-charlestonians/) sought to establish cemeteries where Black communities could honor the dead with dignity. What began regionally — especially in Charleston and Philadelphia – quickly spread nationally during the 19th century across the American South and North.

In the decades after Reconstruction, and especially during the Jim Crow era, nearly [6 million African Americans moved north and west](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/long-lasting-legacy-great-migration-180960118/) to escape racial violence and seek better opportunities – an event known as the Great Migration. This movement often [severed ties between families](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/190696/the-warmth-of-other-suns-by-isabel-wilkerson/) and ancestral burial grounds in the South. As churches and burial societies lost members, many cemeteries fell into disrepair and were [officially labeled “abandoned” by local authorities or developers](https://charlestoncitypaper.com/2008/07/02/hidden-heritage/).

In both rural and urban areas, Black burial grounds were often located on less valuable lands, sites that today are increasingly threatened by gentrification, development and the effects of [climate change](https://yaleclimateconnections.org/2022/11/historic-black-cemeteries-threatened-by-extreme-weather/).

The [Gullah Geechee](https://www.ugapress.org/9780820327839/the-gullah-people-and-their-african-heritage/), who descend from enslaved Africans from West Africa and still preserve unique cultural traditions in the southeastern U.S., argue [these burial sites were never abandoned and that ancestors are still present](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2021/10/04/when-black-history-is-unearthed-who-gets-to-speak-for-the-dead).

This perspective views the dead as actively connected to the living. For them, lacking formally designated cemetery space doesn’t make the sites any less sacred.

## **A tradition of sacred spaces**

For many African Americans, especially in the South, death during slavery was seen as not merely an ending but a spiritual return — a “homegoing.”

Rooted in [West African spiritual worldviews and carried through other traditions in America](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/africanatlantic-cultures-and-the-south-carolina-lowcountry/C02F984E2F2C945B9B945496EF28CE6B), the act of burial was often viewed as a release from bondage, a return to the ancestors and a step toward wholeness.

The Gullah Geechee traditions of coastal South Carolina emphasize ancestral presence, spiritual continuity and the sanctity of the land. In that worldview, with a porous boundary between the living and the dead, proper burial and remembrance are not only cultural imperatives but necessary for community well-being.

It was not until the early 1990s that recognition of rights over ancestral remains and sacred burial grounds began to find a wider audience.

Inspired by the 1990 [Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-43/subtitle-A/part-10) that recognized Indigenous rights over ancestral remains, African American communities increasingly asserted their own rights to ethical research, respectful handling and meaningful memorialization, especially during the 1991 [New York African Burial Ground](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03374233) project, which reshaped public memory and [archaeological ethics](http://www.jstor.org/stable/3069222).

Discovered during construction in lower Manhattan, the 18th-century burial ground contained the remains of more than 400 enslaved and free Africans. Community advocacy led to the site’s protection, descendant-led research, ceremonial reburial and the [establishment of a national memorial in 2006](https://www.nps.gov/afbg/index.htm).

Since this time, across the U.S. and the Atlantic world, descendant-led ceremonies from [Portsmouth, New Hampshire](https://africanburyinggroundnh.org/index.html), to [Key West, Florida](https://www.africanburialgroundathiggsbeach.org/discovery), have restored dignity to ancestral remains.

Meanwhile, efforts to [preserve African American](https://www-nature-com.nuncio.cofc.edu/articles/d41586-021-01320-4) burial grounds, [including by national scholar organizations](https://americananthro.org/about/committees-and-task-forces/tcethr/) and [federal lawmakers](https://adams.house.gov/media-center/press-releases/adams-files-amendment-fund-african-american-burial-grounds-preservation), continue amid political debates over how history should be remembered and taught.

## **What made the Anson Street project unique**

In Charleston, the Anson Street African Burial Ground project stands out for the way Gullah Geechee traditions and descendant collaboration shaped every stage of the process — from scientific study to reinterment.

Launched as a community-led initiative in 2017, the team began by listening. Through regular gatherings, they invited questions about the ancestors’ lives and identities, and about their hopes for the reburial, centering Black community voices at every stage. The team combined [scientific investigations of ancestry and health](https://doi.org/10.1002/ajpa.24149) while also creating space for spiritual guidance, ceremony and descendant leadership.

In doing so, the project became more than a study of the past; it became a communal act of repair and remembrance, [reconnecting Charleston’s present communities with the ancestors whose stories](https://doi.org/10.1017/aaq.2023.105) had long been buried.

Over the next two years, the team wove this commitment into every aspect of its work: youth art programs, a college course on memorial design, public exhibitions, and school partnerships. One of the most moving moments came from conversations with schoolchildren, who decided that the ancestors should be given names before they were reburied.

That naming ceremony took place in April 2019. The names were conferred by [Natalie Washington-Weik, a Yorùbá-Orisa Ọ̀ṣun priestess](http://hdl.handle.net/2152/ETD-UT-2009-08-309), a spiritual leader in a West African tradition and an African historian. She described the ritual as an “important step forward in reclaiming the humanity of the deceased people who were most likely forced to travel across the Atlantic Ocean under the terror of other humans – who saw them merely as animals.”

The ancestors were finally reinterred in a powerful public ceremony that reflected their ancestries and West-Central African spiritual traditions.

## **When pain is acknowledged, healing can occur**

The 2019 naming and reinterment ceremonies were not simply commemorations; they were rituals of remembrance and healing.

Construction for a [permanent memorial](https://www.asabgproject.com/a-memorial-for-the-ancestors) at the Anson Street site, designed by artist Stephen L. Hayes Jr., has now begun. At its center is a basin fabricated with sacred soil collected from 36 African-descended burial grounds across the Charleston region. From the basin, 36 bronze hands will rise – cast from living community members whose profiles reflect those of the ancestors. Raised in gestures of prayer, resistance and reverence, these hands link past to present.

Throughout the memorialization process, community members reflected on what it meant to participate in such a project. Many spoke of feeling pride, reverence, joy, sadness and peace. “This conversation makes me feel complete,” one participant said.

As Charleston demonstrates, these projects are not only about preserving the past – they are acts of recognition, respect and reconciliation, helping communities nationwide confront and honor the histories long denied to African-descended peoples.

# ‘A dog cemetery would not be treated like this’: the fight to preserve Black burial grounds in the US

This article is more than 1 year old

In the absence of federal oversight, Black communities band together to stave off development on historic resting places

![Image 3: Melissa Hellmann](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/uploads/2024/01/24/melissa_hellmann.png?width=75&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)

[Melissa Hellmann](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/melissa-hellmann)

Wed 25 Jun 2025 11.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 25 Jun 2025 11.01 EDT

Share

A large puddle of water and thickets of weeds cover a vacant lot in Bethesda, [Maryland](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/maryland). A towering apartment complex overshadows the cracked asphalt, but Marsha Coleman-Adebayo is most concerned about what – and who – lies beneath.

The nearly two-acre site in the [Washington DC](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/washington-dc) suburb covers the historic Moses Macedonia African Cemetery and another burial ground for [enslaved people](https://www.theguardian.com/world/slavery), with the oldest portion dating back to at least the [mid-1800s](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/22267680-the-bridge-that-carried-us-over/?responsive=1&title=1&mode=document&q=enslaved#document/p41). Hundreds of bones found there may be the remains of enslaved people and their descendants, while [more bodies](https://www.courts.state.md.us/data/opinions/coa/2024/18a23.pdf) may lie under the parking lot of the Westwood Tower apartment complex.

But like many resting grounds for Black Americans, its preservation is jeopardized by loss of its original community through gentrification and, now, encroaching development. And despite a recent federal law to protect Black cemeteries, they are vulnerable to neglect and eventual destruction.

Coleman-Adebayo is the president of the Bethesda African Cemetery Coalition (Bacc), which since 2016 has aimed to save the site from further development and return the land to the descendant community. It plans to eventually erect a museum or monument there. She first learned about the cemetery a year earlier, when she attended a joint county park and planning commission meeting where she met a longtime resident who recalled playing in the long-forgotten cemetery as a child.

![Image 4: Overgrown grass and cracked asphalt with yellow markers.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/bddfb4f4bd89ac0de3f51418dd18daea5288fbbb/0_0_6240_4160/master/6240.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)View image in fullscreen

Overgrown bushes cover part of the former grounds of the Moses Macedonia African Cemetery in Bethesda, Maryland, on 28 May 2025. The area, once a burial site for formerly enslaved African Americans and their descendants, now sits unmarked and unattended. Photograph: Kyna Uwaeme/The Guardian

![Image 5: People with signs and a megaphone.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/601e158d1daef6697e5ed5693d05a8ad60493df3/0_0_6240_4160/master/6240.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)View image in fullscreen

Members of the Bethesda African Cemetery Coalition protest near the Moses Macedonia African Cemetery site in Bethesda, Maryland, on 28 May 2025. The group gathered to raise awareness about the historic Black burial ground, now paved over by a parking lot and threatened by ongoing development. Photograph: Kyna Uwaeme/The Guardian

Every week, Bacc members stage a protest at the McDonald’s parking lot next door. Separated into several parcels, the portion of the burial ground that was leveled for Westwood Tower’s parking lot in the 1960s is now owned by the housing opportunities commission of Montgomery county (HOC), which provides low-income housing. Another part of the cemetery, owned by the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission, is overgrown with vegetation. A third section, held by the self-storage developer 1784 Capital Holdings, has incited ongoing Bacc protests since construction for a storage facility began in 2017. The burial site has turned into a legal battleground as the coalition has spent several years in court fighting the HOC.

The dispute at Moses Macedonia African Cemetery serves to “open up the conversation about what a major problem that African Americans are having at these sites,” said Michael Blakey, a National Endowment for the Humanities professor of anthropology, Africana studies and American studies at the College of William and Mary. For over a decade beginning in the 1990s, Blakey directed the African Burial Ground Project at Howard University, where he and a team of researchers analyzed more than [400 skeletal remains](https://www.wm.edu/sites/1619/news/museum-internl-unesco-pub.pdf) of enslaved and free Africans interred in New York City in the 17th and 18th centuries. His work was guided by the descendants’ questions about their ancestors. “Even when they assert their rights as a descendent community, it’s a wrestling match with bureaucracies, sometimes even anthropologists,” he said.

Burial rites reveal a society’s values in life and in death, Blakey added. “The desecration of Black cemeteries is a reflection, whether in slavery or in current development projects … of the lack of empathy with African Americans as complete human beings,” he said. “And African Americans, from slavery to the present, have defended those cemeteries with sure knowledge of their full humanity and an insistence upon their dignity.”

The Moses Macedonia African Cemetery in Bethesda; the Evergreen Cemetery in St Petersburg, Florida; and the Buena Vista plantation’s burial ground in St James parish, [Louisiana](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/louisiana), demonstrate ongoing fights to preserve Black burial sites in the face of development throughout the US. Amid the scant oversight of Black cemeteries, a growing movement of descendant communities and their allies are protecting the grounds by documenting their existence, protesting development and performing genealogical research on the buried.

## Histories of erasure and exploitation

On a rainy May evening, Coleman-Adebayo held a large white sign listing violations of what she considers a sacred space. “Even a dog cemetery would not be treated like this,” she told the Guardian. As an [Environmental Protection Agency whistleblower](https://www.npr.org/2011/09/06/140214594/high-price-of-blowing-the-whistle-on-epa) who sounded the alarm on US vanadium mining in South Africa in the 1990s, Coleman-Adebayo has a long history of activism. She also helped spearhead the [No Fear Act](https://www.opm.gov/equal-employment-opportunity/no-fear-act/), which discourages retaliation and discrimination in the federal government.

Bacc contends that, during a 2020 excavation, a dump truck took earth from the cemetery to a landfill. Members followed and say they found 30 funerary objects including pieces of cloth, a hair pick and a tombstone. They have also demanded the return of [200 bones](https://bethesdamagazine.com/2023/06/18/boycotting-montgomery-countys-juneteenth-celebration-cemetery-coalition-offers-its-own/) held by a consulting firm in a Gainesville, Virginia, warehouse to no avail. In August, a circuit court will hear a case in which Bacc and several other plaintiffs are requesting [$40m](https://www.arkrepublic.com/2025/04/21/restraining-order-and-countersuit-bacc/)in compensation from the HOC for emotional damage and to build a museum.

![Image 6: A man taking a photo at a construction site, and photos of bones on a poster ](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/db2d25b6c143d95182111337271bde25f70d4b52/0_0_5616_3744/master/5616.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)View image in fullscreen

Left: A possible gravestone was discovered at the construction site in Bethesda, Maryland, in the summer of 2020. Right: Crushed, steamrolled and dismembered bones were found in the Moses cemetery. Photograph: Bethesda African Cemetery Coalition volunteer Nicholas Gregory, Kyna Uwaeme

Coleman-Adebayo looked somberly at the scaffolding erected by self-storage developer 1784 Capital Holdings. “Look what they’re building here on the bodies of African people,” Coleman-Adebayo said. “How did they die? How did they live? What happened to them? And the county could care less because they’re Black.”

The HOC and 1784 Capital Holdings did not respond to requests for comment by publication date.

The River Road community, an African American enclave linked to the cemetery, was a once bustling district with [Black land ownership](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5d8b866f28ac7b58bd12efc2/t/5dd6d03869e9d47fcd6fcce1/1574359105361/forgotten_african_american_community_of_river_road.pdf), a school and the Macedonia Baptist church, which [opened in 1920](https://www.washingtoninformer.com/macedonia-baptist-church-celebrates-100-years/). By the 1950s and 1960s,the area was zoned for commercial use. Now, Coleman-Adebayo’s husband, the Rev Olusegun Adebayo, chairs Bacc’s board and pastors the church, the only surviving institution of the historically Black community.

Black cemeteries have long been threatened. In the 18th century, Blakey said, Black cemeteries were also used to dump waste from pottery factories and tanneries. Historian and anthropologist Lynn Rainville, who has researched Black cemeteries for 20 years, noted that Black bodies were dug up to use as cadavers for 19th-century medical research. But robbers rarely disinterred Black bodies to steal objects or jewelry, as they frequently did to Indigenous burial grounds. After the civil war, Black cemeteries were usually placed in areas with cheaper property values, which later became prime real estate for developers. Some Black cemeteries were also neglected following the great migration of the early 20th century, when 6 million Black people moved from the south to other parts of the US for economic opportunity and to escape racism. As a result, many Black people moved away from their ancestors’ graves.

“The Black living communities have long since been forced out of there because of high taxes, high property values,” Rainville said. “The cemetery is the last of what’s left, and then it is at greatest risk.”

The development at the Moses Macedonia African Cemetery shows that American society values certain bodies over others, said Rainville: “If 2,000 prominent, wealthy people in Bethesda, Maryland, came forward and said, ‘Hey, these are my relatives,’ it would have been stopped by now. No one’s digging up Thomas Jefferson, for example. There is a hierarchy of what and when in American society is considered OK to move.”

During his travels and work throughout the world, Blakey found that development is the paramount threat to Black cemeteries. He recalled discussing with a Howard University colleague in the 1970s about how Black internment sites, he said, “were the places developers were said to be most fond of because they knew they could dispose of them with greater ease”.

## Community-based preservation

A federal law similar to the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), which requires institutions and federal agencies to return human remains and artifacts to their descendant Indigenous tribes, does not exist for Black Americans, said Rainville. Signed into law in the 1990s, the NAGPRA came after hundreds of years of the desecration of Native American graves.

In recent years, a national movement has emerged to protect Black graves by creating a law that parallels the NAGPRA. Enacted into law in 2022, the [African American Burial Grounds Preservation Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/senate-bill/3667) authorized the National Park Service to fund federal and state agencies, as well as non-profits’ efforts, to research and preserve Black cemeteries. But the National Park Service told the Guardian that it has not awarded any grants so far, since Congress has not allocated money to the program.

Seeing a need to prevent the erasure of African American burial grounds in her local community, University of South Florida anthropology chair and professor Antoinette Jackson created the [Black Cemetery Network](https://blackcemeterynetwork.org/), a database of internment sites throughout the US. Of the 193 cemeteries listed on the site, Jackson said that up to 70% of them face preservation challenges, including threats from development, legal battles or lack of resources.

A lack of Black political power in the early 20th century fueled neglect and subsequent loss of cemeteries through tax sales, she added. “It was by design, because many of the ones that were lost were in what became a desirable area for that time,” Jackson said. “Up until the 1965 Civil Rights Act, [Black political] representation wasn’t there in many of these governmental agencies, committees and commissions. So, often, there was no one to defend them, and they were easily given away or changed hands without people really being aware.”

![Image 9: A women holding a sign saying ‘Black Lives Matter in life and in death’](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d572ddec01962063916d03d36f24e1619dad8e99/0_0_3033_4160/master/3033.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)View image in fullscreen

Alexa Sloan, a community organizer with Bacc, joins fellow advocates during a demonstration near the site of the former Moses Macedonia African Cemetery in Bethesda, Maryland, on 28 May 2025. Photograph: Kyna Uwaeme/The Guardian

She cites a [2021 Florida law](https://laws.flrules.org/2021/60) that protects abandoned African American cemeteries as a potential model for other states. The law created a [taskforce](https://dos.fl.gov/historical/archaeology/human-remains/abandoned-cemeteries/2021-abandoned-african-american-cemeteries-task-force/) that identified and researched cemeteries, and led an advisory council that provides recommendations for their preservation. Research and academic institutions, non-profits and local governmental organizations may also apply for [a grant of up to $50,000](https://dos.fl.gov/historical/grants/abandoned-african-american-cemeteries-grants/) to conduct historical and genealogical research, or to restore and maintain abandoned cemeteries.

Jackson [received](https://files.floridados.gov/media/708355/fy2024-aaac-ranking-for-web.pdf) that state grant to find the descendants of the [Evergreen Cemetery](https://blackcemeterynetwork.org/bcnsites/evergreen) – one of three graveyards buried under Interstate 175 and Tropicana Field, a St Petersburg stadium being considered for [redevelopment](https://stpetecatalyst.com/st-pete-forges-ahead-with-gas-plants-redevelopment/#:~:text=The%20wait%20will%20soon%20end,once%20called%20the%20neighborhood%20home.). Through Jackson’s work, St Petersburg city council member Corey Givens Jr learned that his great-great-great-uncle was buried in the historically Black cemetery.

Givens wants the city to conduct a ground-penetrating radar survey of the site to see if any burials remain there. That was done for [Oaklawn Cemetery](https://baynews9.com/content/dam/News/static/pdfs/fl/20241119_Full_Report_Oaklawn_Cemetery_Expanded_GPR_and_Research1-compressed.pdf), where mostly white people were interred and at least [10 possible graves](https://stpetecatalyst.com/report-10-likely-graves-found-at-tropicana-field/) were recently found. But the Florida department of transportation, which owns the property where Evergreen and another Black cemetery, [Moffett](https://blackcemeterynetwork.org/bcnsites/moffett), are located, [has refused](https://www.wtsp.com/article/news/special-reports/erased/florida-house-fdot-search-graves-i-175/67-9d366c75-caed-4d4d-9c62-f40055f36113) to allow a survey.

Givens hopes that the descendants of people interred in Evergreen and Moffett will have a say in the future of the site. “Do we just want to leave these bodies there? Or do we feel like we want to spend tax dollars and move these bodies elsewhere?” Givens told the Guardian. “I really want the community to be in charge of this conversation. I want them to lead it because I don’t trust the same governing body that said ‘out of sight, out of mind’.”

## **Big****oil and a burial site**

At the site of the Buena Vista plantation in St James parish, Louisiana, [the Louisiana Bucket Brigade](https://labucketbrigade.org/) and [Inclusive Louisiana](https://inclusivelouisiana.org/) environmental justice groups are using genealogical research of enslaved people buried on the land to fight the construction of a petrochemical facility.

The Louisiana Bucket Brigade and Inclusive Louisiana learned through a public records request of the Louisiana division of archaeology’s emails that a graveyard for enslaved Africans existed on the land where the Taiwanese company Formosa Plastics planned to construct a [$9.4bn facility](https://www.sunshineprojectla.com/). Lenora Gobert, the Louisiana Bucket Brigade’s genealogist, spent years researching the mortgage and conveyance records from plantation owner Benjamin Winchester to learn the names of the enslaved people buried there between 1820 and 1861. In 2024, the non-profit [released a report](https://labucketbrigade.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/LABB-Final-Buried-at-Buena-Vista-compressed.pdf)detailing the lives of five enslaved people ages nine to 31. Among them was 18-year-old Betsy, who was buried on the plantation’s edge and mortgaged by the Winchesters at least seven times in life and death.

Anne Rolfes, the Louisiana Bucket Brigade’s director, hopes that evidence of the graveyard will help further stall or cancel the development. She would like descendant communities to have a say in how the area is memorialized and programming that honors the area’s history.

“How about we just stop all this petrochemical expansion? It destroys these really sacred places, and it’s not economic development. It’s destruction, massive disruption and illness,” Rolfes told the Guardian. “So let’s instead center this. That would preserve the communities. It would provide so many more jobs. It would be deeply meaningful. It would be a beacon to the rest of the country.”

Meanwhile, in Bethesda, about [100 people](https://www.thebaltimorebanner.com/community/local-news/bethesda-african-cemetery-coalition-juneteenth-LM2SGUOLQ5CCBNII4VD73XS5EY/) attended Bacc’s “rebellion” on 19 June, Coleman-Adebayo said, during which the group featured poetry, dancing and speakers who talked about the struggle to protect the cemetery. [Bacc also protested](https://www.mymcmedia.org/african-cemetery-coalition-pickets-county-juneteenth-event/) at the county’s [Juneteenth event](https://visitmontgomery.com/events/juneteenth/) on 21 June.

At Bacc’s Juneteenth event, member Joann SM Bagnerise received an award for her outstanding advocacy. Bagnerise, an 87-year-old from Dumfries, Virginia, has traveled over an hour each way to join the coalition’s weekly protests for several years. During a recent May protest, she sat in a chair under an umbrella and said: “The desecration of hallowed grounds is un-American.” The high-rise apartment at the center of the dispute towered behind her. “There are young teenagers buried here,” she said. “There are mothers and fathers.”

# ‘A dog cemetery would not be treated like this’: the fight to preserve Black burial grounds in the US

This article is more than 1 year old

In the absence of federal oversight, Black communities band together to stave off development on historic resting places

![Image 3: Melissa Hellmann](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/uploads/2024/01/24/melissa_hellmann.png?width=75&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)

[Melissa Hellmann](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/melissa-hellmann)

Wed 25 Jun 2025 11.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 25 Jun 2025 11.01 EDT

Share

A large puddle of water and thickets of weeds cover a vacant lot in Bethesda, [Maryland](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/maryland). A towering apartment complex overshadows the cracked asphalt, but Marsha Coleman-Adebayo is most concerned about what – and who – lies beneath.

The nearly two-acre site in the [Washington DC](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/washington-dc) suburb covers the historic Moses Macedonia African Cemetery and another burial ground for [enslaved people](https://www.theguardian.com/world/slavery), with the oldest portion dating back to at least the [mid-1800s](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/22267680-the-bridge-that-carried-us-over/?responsive=1&title=1&mode=document&q=enslaved#document/p41). Hundreds of bones found there may be the remains of enslaved people and their descendants, while [more bodies](https://www.courts.state.md.us/data/opinions/coa/2024/18a23.pdf) may lie under the parking lot of the Westwood Tower apartment complex.

But like many resting grounds for Black Americans, its preservation is jeopardized by loss of its original community through gentrification and, now, encroaching development. And despite a recent federal law to protect Black cemeteries, they are vulnerable to neglect and eventual destruction.

Coleman-Adebayo is the president of the Bethesda African Cemetery Coalition (Bacc), which since 2016 has aimed to save the site from further development and return the land to the descendant community. It plans to eventually erect a museum or monument there. She first learned about the cemetery a year earlier, when she attended a joint county park and planning commission meeting where she met a longtime resident who recalled playing in the long-forgotten cemetery as a child.

![Image 4: Overgrown grass and cracked asphalt with yellow markers.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/bddfb4f4bd89ac0de3f51418dd18daea5288fbbb/0_0_6240_4160/master/6240.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)View image in fullscreen

Overgrown bushes cover part of the former grounds of the Moses Macedonia African Cemetery in Bethesda, Maryland, on 28 May 2025. The area, once a burial site for formerly enslaved African Americans and their descendants, now sits unmarked and unattended. Photograph: Kyna Uwaeme/The Guardian

![Image 5: People with signs and a megaphone.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/601e158d1daef6697e5ed5693d05a8ad60493df3/0_0_6240_4160/master/6240.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)View image in fullscreen

Members of the Bethesda African Cemetery Coalition protest near the Moses Macedonia African Cemetery site in Bethesda, Maryland, on 28 May 2025. The group gathered to raise awareness about the historic Black burial ground, now paved over by a parking lot and threatened by ongoing development. Photograph: Kyna Uwaeme/The Guardian

Every week, Bacc members stage a protest at the McDonald’s parking lot next door. Separated into several parcels, the portion of the burial ground that was leveled for Westwood Tower’s parking lot in the 1960s is now owned by the housing opportunities commission of Montgomery county (HOC), which provides low-income housing. Another part of the cemetery, owned by the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission, is overgrown with vegetation. A third section, held by the self-storage developer 1784 Capital Holdings, has incited ongoing Bacc protests since construction for a storage facility began in 2017. The burial site has turned into a legal battleground as the coalition has spent several years in court fighting the HOC.

The dispute at Moses Macedonia African Cemetery serves to “open up the conversation about what a major problem that African Americans are having at these sites,” said Michael Blakey, a National Endowment for the Humanities professor of anthropology, Africana studies and American studies at the College of William and Mary. For over a decade beginning in the 1990s, Blakey directed the African Burial Ground Project at Howard University, where he and a team of researchers analyzed more than [400 skeletal remains](https://www.wm.edu/sites/1619/news/museum-internl-unesco-pub.pdf) of enslaved and free Africans interred in New York City in the 17th and 18th centuries. His work was guided by the descendants’ questions about their ancestors. “Even when they assert their rights as a descendent community, it’s a wrestling match with bureaucracies, sometimes even anthropologists,” he said.

Burial rites reveal a society’s values in life and in death, Blakey added. “The desecration of Black cemeteries is a reflection, whether in slavery or in current development projects … of the lack of empathy with African Americans as complete human beings,” he said. “And African Americans, from slavery to the present, have defended those cemeteries with sure knowledge of their full humanity and an insistence upon their dignity.”

The Moses Macedonia African Cemetery in Bethesda; the Evergreen Cemetery in St Petersburg, Florida; and the Buena Vista plantation’s burial ground in St James parish, [Louisiana](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/louisiana), demonstrate ongoing fights to preserve Black burial sites in the face of development throughout the US. Amid the scant oversight of Black cemeteries, a growing movement of descendant communities and their allies are protecting the grounds by documenting their existence, protesting development and performing genealogical research on the buried.

## Histories of erasure and exploitation

On a rainy May evening, Coleman-Adebayo held a large white sign listing violations of what she considers a sacred space. “Even a dog cemetery would not be treated like this,” she told the Guardian. As an [Environmental Protection Agency whistleblower](https://www.npr.org/2011/09/06/140214594/high-price-of-blowing-the-whistle-on-epa) who sounded the alarm on US vanadium mining in South Africa in the 1990s, Coleman-Adebayo has a long history of activism. She also helped spearhead the [No Fear Act](https://www.opm.gov/equal-employment-opportunity/no-fear-act/), which discourages retaliation and discrimination in the federal government.

Bacc contends that, during a 2020 excavation, a dump truck took earth from the cemetery to a landfill. Members followed and say they found 30 funerary objects including pieces of cloth, a hair pick and a tombstone. They have also demanded the return of [200 bones](https://bethesdamagazine.com/2023/06/18/boycotting-montgomery-countys-juneteenth-celebration-cemetery-coalition-offers-its-own/) held by a consulting firm in a Gainesville, Virginia, warehouse to no avail. In August, a circuit court will hear a case in which Bacc and several other plaintiffs are requesting [$40m](https://www.arkrepublic.com/2025/04/21/restraining-order-and-countersuit-bacc/)in compensation from the HOC for emotional damage and to build a museum.

![Image 6: A man taking a photo at a construction site, and photos of bones on a poster ](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/db2d25b6c143d95182111337271bde25f70d4b52/0_0_5616_3744/master/5616.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)View image in fullscreen

Left: A possible gravestone was discovered at the construction site in Bethesda, Maryland, in the summer of 2020. Right: Crushed, steamrolled and dismembered bones were found in the Moses cemetery. Photograph: Bethesda African Cemetery Coalition volunteer Nicholas Gregory, Kyna Uwaeme

Coleman-Adebayo looked somberly at the scaffolding erected by self-storage developer 1784 Capital Holdings. “Look what they’re building here on the bodies of African people,” Coleman-Adebayo said. “How did they die? How did they live? What happened to them? And the county could care less because they’re Black.”

The HOC and 1784 Capital Holdings did not respond to requests for comment by publication date.

The River Road community, an African American enclave linked to the cemetery, was a once bustling district with [Black land ownership](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5d8b866f28ac7b58bd12efc2/t/5dd6d03869e9d47fcd6fcce1/1574359105361/forgotten_african_american_community_of_river_road.pdf), a school and the Macedonia Baptist church, which [opened in 1920](https://www.washingtoninformer.com/macedonia-baptist-church-celebrates-100-years/). By the 1950s and 1960s,the area was zoned for commercial use. Now, Coleman-Adebayo’s husband, the Rev Olusegun Adebayo, chairs Bacc’s board and pastors the church, the only surviving institution of the historically Black community.

Black cemeteries have long been threatened. In the 18th century, Blakey said, Black cemeteries were also used to dump waste from pottery factories and tanneries. Historian and anthropologist Lynn Rainville, who has researched Black cemeteries for 20 years, noted that Black bodies were dug up to use as cadavers for 19th-century medical research. But robbers rarely disinterred Black bodies to steal objects or jewelry, as they frequently did to Indigenous burial grounds. After the civil war, Black cemeteries were usually placed in areas with cheaper property values, which later became prime real estate for developers. Some Black cemeteries were also neglected following the great migration of the early 20th century, when 6 million Black people moved from the south to other parts of the US for economic opportunity and to escape racism. As a result, many Black people moved away from their ancestors’ graves.

![Image 7: A man and a women standing in a church](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a73df239f72613d126102014ca0d4193db3bab89/0_0_6240_4160/master/6240.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)View image in fullscreen

The Rev Olusegun Adebayo, pastor of the Macedonia Baptist church and chair of the board of the Bethesda African Cemetery Coalition (Bacc), stands with Marsha Coleman-Adebayo, president of Bacc, in Bethesda, Maryland, on 28 May 2025. Photograph: Kyna Uwaeme/The Guardian

![Image 8: A small church ](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/88b077bc829fba05060194e5b3322ed35ae42ee6/0_0_6240_4160/master/6240.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)View image in fullscreen

The grounds of the Macedonia Baptist church. The only surviving institution of the historically Black community, the church has become a focal point in the fight to preserve the Moses Macedonia African Cemetery, a burial ground threatened by nearby development. Photograph: Kyna Uwaeme/The Guardian

“The Black living communities have long since been forced out of there because of high taxes, high property values,” Rainville said. “The cemetery is the last of what’s left, and then it is at greatest risk.”

The development at the Moses Macedonia African Cemetery shows that American society values certain bodies over others, said Rainville: “If 2,000 prominent, wealthy people in Bethesda, Maryland, came forward and said, ‘Hey, these are my relatives,’ it would have been stopped by now. No one’s digging up Thomas Jefferson, for example. There is a hierarchy of what and when in American society is considered OK to move.”

During his travels and work throughout the world, Blakey found that development is the paramount threat to Black cemeteries. He recalled discussing with a Howard University colleague in the 1970s about how Black internment sites, he said, “were the places developers were said to be most fond of because they knew they could dispose of them with greater ease”.

## Community-based preservation

A federal law similar to the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA), which requires institutions and federal agencies to return human remains and artifacts to their descendant Indigenous tribes, does not exist for Black Americans, said Rainville. Signed into law in the 1990s, the NAGPRA came after hundreds of years of the desecration of Native American graves.

In recent years, a national movement has emerged to protect Black graves by creating a law that parallels the NAGPRA. Enacted into law in 2022, the [African American Burial Grounds Preservation Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/senate-bill/3667) authorized the National Park Service to fund federal and state agencies, as well as non-profits’ efforts, to research and preserve Black cemeteries. But the National Park Service told the Guardian that it has not awarded any grants so far, since Congress has not allocated money to the program.

Seeing a need to prevent the erasure of African American burial grounds in her local community, University of South Florida anthropology chair and professor Antoinette Jackson created the [Black Cemetery Network](https://blackcemeterynetwork.org/), a database of internment sites throughout the US. Of the 193 cemeteries listed on the site, Jackson said that up to 70% of them face preservation challenges, including threats from development, legal battles or lack of resources.

A lack of Black political power in the early 20th century fueled neglect and subsequent loss of cemeteries through tax sales, she added. “It was by design, because many of the ones that were lost were in what became a desirable area for that time,” Jackson said. “Up until the 1965 Civil Rights Act, [Black political] representation wasn’t there in many of these governmental agencies, committees and commissions. So, often, there was no one to defend them, and they were easily given away or changed hands without people really being aware.”

![Image 9: A women holding a sign saying ‘Black Lives Matter in life and in death’](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d572ddec01962063916d03d36f24e1619dad8e99/0_0_3033_4160/master/3033.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)View image in fullscreen

Alexa Sloan, a community organizer with Bacc, joins fellow advocates during a demonstration near the site of the former Moses Macedonia African Cemetery in Bethesda, Maryland, on 28 May 2025. Photograph: Kyna Uwaeme/The Guardian

She cites a [2021 Florida law](https://laws.flrules.org/2021/60) that protects abandoned African American cemeteries as a potential model for other states. The law created a [taskforce](https://dos.fl.gov/historical/archaeology/human-remains/abandoned-cemeteries/2021-abandoned-african-american-cemeteries-task-force/) that identified and researched cemeteries, and led an advisory council that provides recommendations for their preservation. Research and academic institutions, non-profits and local governmental organizations may also apply for [a grant of up to $50,000](https://dos.fl.gov/historical/grants/abandoned-african-american-cemeteries-grants/) to conduct historical and genealogical research, or to restore and maintain abandoned cemeteries.

Jackson [received](https://files.floridados.gov/media/708355/fy2024-aaac-ranking-for-web.pdf) that state grant to find the descendants of the [Evergreen Cemetery](https://blackcemeterynetwork.org/bcnsites/evergreen) – one of three graveyards buried under Interstate 175 and Tropicana Field, a St Petersburg stadium being considered for [redevelopment](https://stpetecatalyst.com/st-pete-forges-ahead-with-gas-plants-redevelopment/#:~:text=The%20wait%20will%20soon%20end,once%20called%20the%20neighborhood%20home.). Through Jackson’s work, St Petersburg city council member Corey Givens Jr learned that his great-great-great-uncle was buried in the historically Black cemetery.

Givens wants the city to conduct a ground-penetrating radar survey of the site to see if any burials remain there. That was done for [Oaklawn Cemetery](https://baynews9.com/content/dam/News/static/pdfs/fl/20241119_Full_Report_Oaklawn_Cemetery_Expanded_GPR_and_Research1-compressed.pdf), where mostly white people were interred and at least [10 possible graves](https://stpetecatalyst.com/report-10-likely-graves-found-at-tropicana-field/) were recently found. But the Florida department of transportation, which owns the property where Evergreen and another Black cemetery, [Moffett](https://blackcemeterynetwork.org/bcnsites/moffett), are located, [has refused](https://www.wtsp.com/article/news/special-reports/erased/florida-house-fdot-search-graves-i-175/67-9d366c75-caed-4d4d-9c62-f40055f36113) to allow a survey.

Givens hopes that the descendants of people interred in Evergreen and Moffett will have a say in the future of the site. “Do we just want to leave these bodies there? Or do we feel like we want to spend tax dollars and move these bodies elsewhere?” Givens told the Guardian. “I really want the community to be in charge of this conversation. I want them to lead it because I don’t trust the same governing body that said ‘out of sight, out of mind’.”

## **Big****oil and a burial site**

At the site of the Buena Vista plantation in St James parish, Louisiana, [the Louisiana Bucket Brigade](https://labucketbrigade.org/) and [Inclusive Louisiana](https://inclusivelouisiana.org/) environmental justice groups are using genealogical research of enslaved people buried on the land to fight the construction of a petrochemical facility.

The Louisiana Bucket Brigade and Inclusive Louisiana learned through a public records request of the Louisiana division of archaeology’s emails that a graveyard for enslaved Africans existed on the land where the Taiwanese company Formosa Plastics planned to construct a [$9.4bn facility](https://www.sunshineprojectla.com/). Lenora Gobert, the Louisiana Bucket Brigade’s genealogist, spent years researching the mortgage and conveyance records from plantation owner Benjamin Winchester to learn the names of the enslaved people buried there between 1820 and 1861. In 2024, the non-profit [released a report](https://labucketbrigade.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/LABB-Final-Buried-at-Buena-Vista-compressed.pdf)detailing the lives of five enslaved people ages nine to 31. Among them was 18-year-old Betsy, who was buried on the plantation’s edge and mortgaged by the Winchesters at least seven times in life and death.

Anne Rolfes, the Louisiana Bucket Brigade’s director, hopes that evidence of the graveyard will help further stall or cancel the development. She would like descendant communities to have a say in how the area is memorialized and programming that honors the area’s history.

![Image 10: A sign on a fence ](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/80dc07dbecf3787a514783a4fafbdc6fdd4cc301/0_0_6240_4160/master/6240.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)View image in fullscreen

A sign marks the location near the former Moses Macedonia African Cemetery in Bethesda, Maryland. Photograph: Kyna Uwaeme/The Guardian

![Image 11: Water pools on cracked concrete surrounded by overgrown vegetation ](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/703250f58f4e72381330fdea2036262f4a1bccd9/0_0_6240_4160/master/6240.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)View image in fullscreen

Water discharges on to the grounds where the Moses Macedonia African Cemetery once stood. Photograph: Kyna Uwaeme/The Guardian

“How about we just stop all this petrochemical expansion? It destroys these really sacred places, and it’s not economic development. It’s destruction, massive disruption and illness,” Rolfes told the Guardian. “So let’s instead center this. That would preserve the communities. It would provide so many more jobs. It would be deeply meaningful. It would be a beacon to the rest of the country.”

Meanwhile, in Bethesda, about [100 people](https://www.thebaltimorebanner.com/community/local-news/bethesda-african-cemetery-coalition-juneteenth-LM2SGUOLQ5CCBNII4VD73XS5EY/) attended Bacc’s “rebellion” on 19 June, Coleman-Adebayo said, during which the group featured poetry, dancing and speakers who talked about the struggle to protect the cemetery. [Bacc also protested](https://www.mymcmedia.org/african-cemetery-coalition-pickets-county-juneteenth-event/) at the county’s [Juneteenth event](https://visitmontgomery.com/events/juneteenth/) on 21 June.

At Bacc’s Juneteenth event, member Joann SM Bagnerise received an award for her outstanding advocacy. Bagnerise, an 87-year-old from Dumfries, Virginia, has traveled over an hour each way to join the coalition’s weekly protests for several years. During a recent May protest, she sat in a chair under an umbrella and said: “The desecration of hallowed grounds is un-American.” The high-rise apartment at the center of the dispute towered behind her. “There are young teenagers buried here,” she said. “There are mothers and fathers.”

# National Park Service – African Burial Ground

![Image 2](https://cushareejournal.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/pic5-e1539204915480.jpg?w=1070)

![Image 3: pic 1](https://cushareejournal.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/pic-1.jpg?w=736)

Image 1: (Photo credit: NPS)

Among all the history that occupies lower Manhattan, including Wall Street, Trinity Church, and the 9/11 Memorial, only one site has been designated as a National Monument: the African Burial Ground. This 0.35 acre memorial and museum marks the resting place of over 10,000 Africans and African Americans. Originally occupying over 6 acres, the cemetery served New York’s free and enslaved African community between 1690 and 1794. This short introduction to the African Burial Ground will focus on the recent archaeological history of the site.

With over a hundred years of burials, and close proximity to other Colonial Era sites, it is surprising that the African Burial Ground was essentially lost from public memory for nearly 200 years. Although forgotten, the cemetery could not be ignored: it was disturbed multiple times throughout the 19 th century by the construction of department stores, homes, and offices. The churned up human bone was either ignored or looted, with few questions raised to why remains were there. It wasn’t until much later, at the end of the 20 th century, that the African Burial Ground received the archaeological investigation it deserved.

With the constant urban renovation of New York City, the re-discovery of this important site was inevitably construction-led. A government office building was to be erected, and United States law requires archaeological assessments be carried out for federal construction projects. Although the area was likely identified during the desk assessment as the “Negros Burial Ground” it was assumed that there would be no intact burials given the amount of development that had occurred in the preceding 200 years.

![Image 4: pic 2](https://cushareejournal.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/pic-2.jpg?w=736)

Image 2: (Photo Credit: Library of Congress)

Advertisement

Archaeological survey, however, identified multiple burials 30 meters below the current ground level. Excavation was overseen by the General Services Administration (GSA), who announced the discovery in October 1991. Immediately, questions were raised as to whether the GSA was properly handling the remains now in its care. The original excavation plan was to expose, record, and remove the entire cemetery, but this plan was soon revised due to the size of the site, which exceeded the limits of the construction area. The African American community was understandably concerned that the remains of their ancestors were not being treated with respect and that the project design did not adequately address the importance of the site. Despite circulation of the initial archaeological survey reports, the project design had not consulted the African American community or academic experts in African Diaspora studies. Protests were staged throughout 1992, particularly in response to the news that some otherwise complete burials had been transected and broken by the archaeologists. The activists’ expectations were reasonable: protect, respect, and study – thoroughly – the remains being exhumed. Their work lead to a Public Works hearing, which resulted in control of the site being transferred to biological anthropologist Michael Blakey and colleagues at Howard University. The choice of Howard University was significant given its status as a Historically Black College, ensuring members of the African American community would be directing the study of their ancestors. The activists were also able to successfully lobby the United States Congress to alter the plans for the federal building, removing the portion that sat directly over where the remains were found. The area was then reserved for the construction of a memorial, the cost of which was worked into the federal budget. The design of the memorial began with a competition in 1998. Rodney Leon and Nicole Hollant-Denis of AARRIS Architects submitted the winning design, centering around an Ancestral Chamber and incorporating symbols of the African Diaspora.

[![Image 5: Image 3: (Photo credit: author)](https://i0.wp.com/cushareejournal.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/pic-3.jpg?w=364&h=273&ssl=1)](https://cushareejournal.wordpress.com/2018/10/12/national-park-service-african-burial-ground/pic-3/)

 Image 3: (Photo credit: author) 

[![Image 6: Image 4: (Photo credit: author)](https://i0.wp.com/cushareejournal.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/pic4.jpg?w=364&h=273&ssl=1)](https://cushareejournal.wordpress.com/2018/10/12/national-park-service-african-burial-ground/pic4/)

 Image 4: (Photo credit: author) 

By November 1993, 420 graves were excavated, with 419 individuals represented by human remains. Ten years later, following the completion of osteological examination of all 419 individuals, the remains were to be reinterred. Each person was placed in a hand-carved coffin, styled with West African motifs in honour of the ancestral birthplace of those buried in the cemetery.

![Image 7: pic5](https://cushareejournal.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/pic5-e1539204915480.jpg?w=277&h=370)

Image 5: (Photo credit: author)

They were placed in seven groups and buried under mounds at the Burial Ground site in October of 2003 [IMAGE 5]. In 2006, then-president George W. Bush designated the site as a National Monument.

The Ancestral Chamber, with its seven elements, was completed in 2007. The Wall of Remembrance is the first feature visitors see, setting the tone for the experience of reflection and education [IMAGE 6].

Advertisement

Opposite is the Memorial Wall that contextualises the Monument and the historical cemetery, forming part of the Ancestral Chamber. In the architect’s words, “The Ancestral Chamber is intended to reflect African cultural, spiritual and ancestral essence. The spiritual form rises out of the ground like an ancestral pillar and represents the soaring African spirit embracing and comforting all who enter.”

![Image 8: pic6](https://cushareejournal.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/pic6.jpg?w=736)

Image 6: (Photo credit: NPS)

![Image 9: pic 7](https://cushareejournal.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/pic-7.png?w=736)

Image 7: (Photo credit: NPS)

[IMAGE 7] Signifying the connection and movement between the spiritual and physical realms, the Spiral Processional Ramp leads from the Ancestral Chamber to the Ancestral Libation Court. The Ancestral Libation Court is a cultural space for present-day public ceremonies, located below street level close the original level of the burial ground. It is surrounded by the Circle of the Diaspora, a wall engraved with multi-cultural symbols of the African Diaspora, divinity, faith, understanding, cemetery guardians, and ancestral learning.

![Image 10: pic 8](https://cushareejournal.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/pic-8.png?w=736)

Image 8: (Photo credit: NPS)

[IMAGE 8] In the foreground of all these meaningful elements lays the Ancestral Re-Interment Grove, the location of the seven burial mounds which has become the resting place for all those disturbed by the excavation. It also shelters the monument from the adjacent building by seven trees, and surrounds to the Ancestral Chamber.

In 2010, the National Park Service opened a visitor centre, which details the history of the site, its excavation, conclusions from the bioarchaeological investigation, and civic engagement at the site, as well as the broader history and lives of Africans and African Americans in colonial New York.

The African Burial Ground represents a part of United States history that is often glossed over in public memory. Its designation as a National Monument draws into focus the presence of Africans in colonial America and centralizes the lived experiences of the people who made up the African Community in New York. The study of the excavated artefacts and human remains had a rocky start, but the effort of the present day African American community resulted in a thorough and respectful examination. Hopefully, it will serve as an example for future studies, so that the descendant populations of future archaeological work in America will be included in project design from the beginning.

Along with European merchants, traders, sailors and farmers, these enslaved workers helped to establish the early colony. Throughout the 17th and 18th centuries, Africans were an important part of the city’s population, reaching a peak of over twenty percent. The African Burial Ground National Monument memorial will be open to the public every day from 9:00 am to 5:00 pm except New Year’s, Christmas and Thanksgiving. In 1993, the site was preserved as a National Historic Landmark by the Secretary of the Interior and was later designated a National Monument by Presidential Proclamation on February 27, 2006. In June, 2004 NPS convened the five finalist designers for a series of public forums in New York City’s five boroughs. The finalists presented their designs for public comment and each designer revised their designs based on public feedback from these presentations. Throughout September 2004, the public was able to see the completed designs and comment on them at six locations in New York City’s five boroughs, as well as online. The GSA and the NPS gathered public feedback on the finalist memorial designs through the African Burial Ground Web site (www.africanburialground.gov), special exhibits and public forums. “The memorial represents a unique opportunity and responsibility for all of us,” said Rodney Léon. “No longer will one walk past this site or through Lower Manhattan and not be provided the opportunity to know, understand, and acknowledge and respect the significance of this site.” The first Africans arrived in New Amsterdam about 1625. Along with European merchants, traders, sailors and farmers, these enslaved workers helped to establish the early colony. Throughout the 17th and 18th centuries, Africans were an important part of the city’s population, reaching a peak of over twenty percent. The African Burial Ground tells the story of the contributions of enslaved and free Africans in the life and building of the early Dutch colony of New Amsterdam, which would later become New York City. The history of the site reveals how New York played an early and critical role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade. It is the newest national monument in New York City, joining the Statue of Liberty, Governors Island, and Castle Clinton. “There is no other national monument in our country that addresses either slavery or the early African-American experience, and we are honored to be home of this tribute to those who lived and died here,” said Mayor Michael Bloomberg. “It is our hope that those who visit this monument will be reminded of how far we have come, and may the memory of those buried here be forever honored.” The opening of the new memorial is the result of an ongoing partnership between the public and private sectors dating to the rediscovery of the site. An advisory group, the African Burial Ground Federal Steering Committee, provided recommendations to assist in planning for the site. The dedication ceremony is the inaugural co-sponsorship event of the African Burial Ground Monument Foundation, the park’s official non-profit partner, and the National Park Service. In addition, New York City Council Speaker Christine Quinn and Manhattan Borough President Scott Stringer hosted the pre-dedication breakfast for speakers and special guests. “This is a critical milestone in the evolution of the African Burial Ground project, but more a beginning than a culmination,” said Howard Dodson, secretary of the African Burial Ground Monument Foundation. “The monument and the interpretive center that will support it are important new resources for commemorating and telling the stories of our enslaved colonial African ancestors.” The African Burial Ground was designated by President Bush as a national monument in February 2006, making it the 390th national park site to be managed by the National Park Service, an agency of the U.S. Department of the Interior. The African Burial Ground National Monument memorial will be open to the public every day from 9:00 am to 5:00 pm except New Year’s, Christmas and Thanksgiving. The visitor center, located in 290 Broadway, will be open Monday to Friday 9:00 am to 5:00 pm except for federal holidays. “The African Burial Ground National Monument is a significant addition to the National Park System,” said Dennis Reidenbach, Northeast regional director of the National Park Service. “We must tell the stories of all Americans and the burial ground is a place where we reach into the past and have an opportunity to touch the future by telling the stories of the Africans who worked to make New York City and the nation strong.” **About the****African****Burial****Ground****National Monument****([www.nps.gov/afbg](http://www.nps.gov/afbg))** One of the most significant archaeological finds in U.S. history, the African Burial Ground is a 17th and 18th century cemetery that was re-discovered in 1991 when construction began on a federal office building in Lower Manhattan. In 1993, the site was preserved as a National Historic Landmark by the Secretary of the Interior and was later designated a National Monument by Presidential Proclamation on February 27, 2006. The National Monument is part of an original seven-acre site containing the remains of approximately 15,000 people, making it the largest and oldest African cemetery excavated in North America. **About the****African****Burial****Ground****Monument****Foundation** The African Burial Ground Monument Foundation was established in 2006 by Dr. James Forbes, Senior Minister Emeritus, The Riverside Church, Edward Lewis, Chairman and Founder of Essence Communications Inc. and Howard Dodson, Director, The Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, with the objectives of raising funds and generating global outreach for America’s newest National Monument. | | | [**—DOI—**](https://www.doi.gov/sites/default/files/archive/news/index.html) * * * [Accessibility](https://www.doi.gov/sites/default/files/archive/news/accessibility.html)|[Feedback](https://www.doi.gov/sites/default/files/archive/news/feedback.html)|[Notices](https://www.doi.gov/sites/default/files/archive/news/notices/index.html)|[Disclaimer](https://www.doi.gov/sites/default/files/archive/news/disclaimer.html)|[Privacy Statement](https://www.doi.gov/sites/default/files/archive/news/privacy.html)|[FOIA](http://www.doi.gov/foia/)|[E-Gov](http://www.whitehouse.gov/omb/egov/)|[USA.gov](http://www.usa.gov/)|[DOI Home](https://www.doi.gov/sites/default/files/archive/news/index.html) U.S. Department of the Interior 1849 C Street, NW Washington, DC 20240 [feedback@ios.doi.gov](mailto:feedback@ios.doi.gov) Last Updated on 10/09/07

I’m revisiting a video I made years ago on one of the most important archeological finds in Manhattan, the African Burial Ground. This originally six acre site was the final resting place of enslaved and free Africans beginning in New Amsterdam and later New York, before the northward expansion of the city swallowed it up. In the 90s it was rediscovered and thanks to the tireless work of activists, we have the memorial you see today.
