The differences that are apparent between enamel and bone samples from the same individual suggests that bone shows some isotopic exchange with the TIDC surface waters. This rejuvenation results in an average decrease in age of 250 years, a minor difference for dates in the early and mid-Holocene. The isotopic exchange of carbon, in addition, does not seem to be linked to time (e.g. 8420 and 8470 BP), but rather to local variation in inundation or sediment. The δ 13 C from bones that experienced early diagenesis remains slightly more positive (e.g. G1B8), but this criterion is too tenuous to be reliable.


Convergence of dates based on multiple sources was also used to evaluate the age of features such as the middens or lakebed fauna. Clam shell from middens or the lakebed that was sampled in multiple ways (leached; chalky exterior shell; dense opalescent, unaltered inner shell) yielded generally concordant results.


In conclusion, dating of the bone and enamel bioapatite has provided the backbone for our chronology (Figure 2). If significant diagenesis were a confounding factor, the dates would show greater dispersion.


### Comparative Craniometric Analysis


Craniometric measurements were selected to provide maximum correspondence with previous work on North African Late Pleistocene and Holocene human remains [[18]](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0002995#pone.0002995-Dutour1), [[26]](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0002995#pone.0002995-Chamla1), [[27]](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0002995#pone.0002995-Mauny1). Seven chronospatial sample units were defined in accordance with published radiometric dates and allocation of specific sites to particular North African cultures (Table 3, numbers 1–7). The principal components analysis includes all individuals for which data were available and the maximum number of craniometric variables. After individuals were allocated to one of the sampling units, variable means were calculated from the raw data for the following variables: LGO, BPX, LBN, HBB, AFR, APA, AOC, CFR, COC, HNP, HNZ, BNZ, BZY, BFW, BFX, HORC (Table 4). The resulting matrix of means was subjected to principal components analysis to capture the correlations among variable means in a more manageable number of dimensions (Figure 6). The strength of this approach is that it allows maximum inclusion of individuals and variables and thus captures the greatest possible genotypic structure. This approach, however, does not consider within-sample variability, and population affinity is based solely on mean differences.


Three of the loadings from the principal components analysis returned eigenvalues greater than 1.0 (Table 7). Factor loadings transparently reflect anatomical or functional units. The first principal component appears to most closely approximate a size vector, but the loadings are not uniformly positive. The pattern of positive and negative loadings for principal components 2 and 3 are not interpretable.

### Strontium Isotope Analysis


In order to investigate residential mobility and sedentism at the Gobero site complex, strontium isotope analysis was performed on archaeological human tooth enamel as well as modern baseline soil and faunal samples. At the Archaeological Chemistry Laboratory at Arizona State University (ASU), the teeth and bone samples were first mechanically cleaned by abrasion with a Dremel 3956-02 Variable Speed MultiPro drill equipped with an engraving cutter to remove the outermost layers of tooth enamel, which are most susceptible to diagenetic contamination. Eight milligrams of tooth enamel powder were dissolved in 0.50 mL of twice-distilled 5 M HNO 3. Bone and soil samples were ashed at 800°C for 10 hours, and then soil samples were digested in concentrated HF and HNO 3.


The strontium, uranium and neodymium concentrations were separated from the sample matrix in the W.M. Keck Foundation Laboratory for Environmental Biogeochemistry (ASU). The strontium was separated using EiChrom SrSpec resin, a crown-ether Sr-selective resin (100–15 µm diameter) loaded into the tip of a glass column. The SrSpec resin was pre-soaked and flushed with H 2 O to remove strontium present from the resin manufacturing process. The resin was further cleaned in the column with repeated washes of deionized H 2 O and conditioned with 750 µL of HNO 3. The dissolved sample was loaded in 250 µL of 5 M HNO 3, washed in 500 µL of 5 M HNO 3, and then the strontium was eluted with 1000 µL of H 2 O. Samples were analyzed using the Neptune multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (MC-ICP-MS). Recent 87 Sr/86 Sr analyses of strontium carbonate standard SRM-987 yield a value of 87 Sr/86 Sr = 0.710261±0.000020 (2σ), which is in agreement with analyses of SRM-987 using a thermal ionization mass spectrometer (TIMS), where 87 Sr/86 Sr = 0.710263±0.000016 (2σ) [[45]](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0002995#pone.0002995-Sato1).


Uranium and neodymium concentrations were obtained on a quadrupole inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometer (Q-ICP-MS) to monitor diagenetic contamination in the samples. Since biogenic enamel and bone should have very low concentrations of these elements, elevated concentrations of uranium and neodymium can be used as proxies for the presence of diagenetic contamination of trace elements such as strontium. The mean U/Ca and Nd/Ca ratios are low and within the range of published uncontaminated U/Ca ratios from enamel samples (U/Ca = 1.08×10−6±1.33×10−6, n = 7, 1σ; Nd/Ca = 3.73×10−7±3.94×10−7, n = 7, 1σ).


Baseline strontium isotope data from soil samples soil samples colleccted from burials show that 87 Sr/86 Sr = 0.71290±0.00064 (n = 7, 1σ), and modern faunal samples exhibit 87 Sr/86 Sr = 0.71261±0.00116 (n = 21, 1σ) (Table 8). **Sleepy Hollow Cemetery** in [Sleepy Hollow, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow,_New_York "Sleepy Hollow, New York"), United States,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-4) is a non-profit, non-sectarian burying ground of about 90 acres (36 ha).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-SH-Famous-5) It is the [final resting place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemetery "Cemetery") of numerous famous figures, including [Washington Irving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Irving "Washington Irving"), who was a cofounder of the establishment. Incorporated in 1849 as Tarrytown Cemetery, it was renamed Sleepy Hollow Cemetery in 1865.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:1-6)

The cemetery is contiguous with, but separate from, the [Burial Ground of the](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch_Church_of_Sleepy_Hollow#Old_Dutch_Burying_Ground "Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow")[Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch_Church_of_Sleepy_Hollow "Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow"), which was a setting for Washington Irving's famous story, _[The Legend of Sleepy Hollow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Sleepy\_Hollow "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow")_. The [Rockefeller family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_family "Rockefeller family") estate, [Kykuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kykuit "Kykuit"), whose grounds abut Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, contains the private Rockefeller cemetery,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:3-7) which is located behind a high fence at the north end of Sleepy Hollow Cemetery.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:2-8)

Sleepy Hollow Cemetery was listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") in 2009.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-NRHP2009-2)

## History and design

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and design")]

In 1847, the [New York State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Legislature "New York State Legislature") passed the [Rural Cemetery Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_Cemetery_Act "Rural Cemetery Act"), which authorized commercial burial grounds in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). The law led to the burial of human remains becoming a commercial business for the first time, replacing the practice of burying the dead in churchyards or on private farmland. Almost immediately after that, a group of prominent local residents, headed by author Washington Irving and Capt. [Jacob Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirck_Storm#Jacob_Storm "Dirck Storm") initiated the building of a modern burial ground in the [Tarrytown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarrytown,_New_York "Tarrytown, New York") area,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-10) as the Burying Ground at the Old Dutch Church no longer had adequate burial space for the growing community.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-11) Tarrytown Cemetery was incorporated on October 29, 1849. On April 11, 1865, it would be officially renamed Sleepy Hollow Cemetery—the name on which Washington Irving had insisted from the beginning, but was initially overruled.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:1-6) The new cemetery began with 39 acres north of the church graveyard, subsequently growing by about 41 acres in 1886 and an additional 10 acres in 1890.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-12)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-size-1)

It was designed as a [garden—or rural—cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_cemetery "Rural cemetery"), a style that was popular in the United States and Europe during the mid-19th century. (Washington Irving was a strong proponent of the garden cemetery movement.) Jim Logan, superintendent of Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, writes on his website, _Sleepy Hollow Country_: "Think of it as the Victorian version of therapeutic landscape architecture—a place where grief could unfold amid natural beauty rather than urban gloom."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:1-6)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-13)

The building of this type of cemetery involved well-planned walkways and elaborately landscaped plantings of trees and shrubs.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-14) The Tarrytown/Sleepy Hollow area, with its rolling hills, old-growth trees, and the gently flowing [Pocantico River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocantico_River "Pocantico River"), was a perfect location for a garden cemetery. Before the widespread development of [public parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_park "Urban park"), Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, like other garden cemeteries, provided a place for the public to enjoy outdoor recreation in a park-like setting. In the 21st century, it is still a popular spot for locals to take a nature walk.

Names of prominent local families are found on stone-fronted family vaults built into the hillsides in the older section of the cemetery, but most of the burials are family plots with multiple tombstones. In the northern section, on the higher elevations, there are numerous mausoleums and large plots with elaborate monuments of "many New York achievers"[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-15) of the [Gilded Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilded_Age "Gilded Age").

The cemetery's historic **Hillside [Receiving Vault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiving_vault "Receiving vault")** provided essential "cold storage" before the advent of modern [steam shovels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_shovel "Steam shovel") and [backhoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backhoe "Backhoe"). Built directly into a steep hillside, the solid masonry structure used the earth's natural insulation to hold bodies when the ground was too frozen for burial. It is a contributing structure to the cemetery's 2009 listing on the National Register of Historic Places.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-16) The vault gained international fame as the crypt of Barnabas Collins in the 1970 film _[House of Dark Shadows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House\_of\_Dark\_Shadows "House of Dark Shadows")_. No longer used for mass winter storage, it is part of official cemetery tours.

**Purported "Headless Horseman" cemetery bridge.** A popular feature is the cemetery’s rustic bridge over a Pocantico River ravine, near a small waterfall and the river’s natural Cascade Pool. Cemetery superintendent Jim Logan writes: "Visitors have long associated it with the famous bridge from Irving’s tale, though it’s a much later addition to the landscape. Still, there’s something fitting about it—a wooden span over running water, framed by autumn foliage, that captures the atmosphere of Irving’s story even if it wasn’t part of his original inspiration."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:1-6)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-17)

The modest **[Washington Irving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Irving "Washington Irving")'s gravestone** (1859) is located in the Irving family plot, where his parents, brothers (including [Peter Irving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Irving "Peter Irving")), nephews, and nieces are also buried. According to his nephew and literary assistant, Pierre Munroe Irving, the author had selected the specific place next to his mother when visiting the cemetery several days before his death.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-18) Creating a unique literary landmark, the author is buried close to the historic [Burying Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch_Church_of_Sleepy_Hollow#Old_Dutch_Burying_Ground "Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow") of the [Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch_Church_of_Sleepy_Hollow "Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow"), where the graves of people who inspired _[The Legend of Sleepy Hollow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Sleepy\_Hollow "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow")_ characters are located.

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/WashingtonIrvingGrave.jpg/250px-WashingtonIrvingGrave.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WashingtonIrvingGrave.jpg)

Headstone of [Washington Irving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Irving "Washington Irving")

The 1926 gravestone index, _The Old Dutch Burying Ground of Sleepy Hollow,_ describes it as follows:[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:22-19)

> On the Northern edge of the burying ground, overlooking his beloved .... Hollow, rest the remains of the gentle Washington Irving: the shrine of thousands of pilgrims from the distant places of the earth. Marked by no tawdry memorial of elaborate sculpture, a simple marble slab indicates the grave; a slab ingeniously fashioned, with rounded comers and edges designed to foil souvenir collectors who have carried off piece-meal two earlier stones.

While earlier grave decorations in the Old Dutch Burying Ground were carved from [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone"), Irving’s gravestone was made from white [marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble "Marble"). It became the preferred material for [Neoclassical architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") and decoration of the post-Revolutionary period, chosen for its association with the purity and idealized forms of [ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_art "Ancient Greek art") and [Roman art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_art "Roman art"). Marble, however, proved to be a rather poor choice for exterior monuments: originally smooth and glistening, marble surfaces soften with time and become rough, grainy, and discolored.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-20) Also, like sandstone, marble is easy to chip. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it was a common, though destructive, practice for tourists to chip off small pieces of sandstone and marble grave markers of famous people as souvenirs.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-21) The Irving gravestone that people see today is the third iteration of the original grave marker; as mentioned above, souvenir hunters chipped away at previous ones, which eventually had to be replaced. (By the end of the 19th century, newly developed power tools would make it practicable to carve gravestones and monuments out of durable [granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-22))

Irving's gravestone is the most visited place in the cemetery. In the words of the [New York Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Supreme_Court "New York Supreme Court") justice [Isaac N. Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_N._Mills "Isaac N. Mills"):[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:0-23)

> Sleepy Hollow... The genius of Irving, whose remains, at his own request, rest within her soil, that sweet and gentle Father of American Literature, has made her name known and loved, as far and as widely as the English tongue is spoken.

**Darius Ogden Mills Mausoleum** (1883), designed by the famous architect [Richard Morris Hunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Morris_Hunt "Richard Morris Hunt"), was commissioned and built decades before [Darius Ogden Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darius_Ogden_Mills "Darius Ogden Mills")' death in 1910. Its construction coincided with the height of the [Gilded Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilded_Age "Gilded Age"), a period when wealthy industrial families built increasingly elaborate monuments in garden cemeteries such as Sleepy Hollow Cemetery. A [Roman temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_temple "Roman temple")-like structure with grand [Ionic columns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_order "Ionic order"), it reflects the [Neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") and [Beaux-Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaux-Arts_architecture "Beaux-Arts architecture") styles favored by the era's elite. Unlike many traditional mausoleums, it is noted for having large, floor-to-ceiling windows on each side and in the roof, designed to capture light and highlight the silver-painted stars on the walls and floors; it creates a play of light that symbolizes eternal life and celestial presence. Visitors can see the ornate [sarcophagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus "Sarcophagus") and interior decorations without entering, a rare feature in 19th-century funerary architecture.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-24)

The monument of Owen Jones (1884) is an example of [Gothic Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_Revival_decorative_arts "Gothic Revival decorative arts") architecture, adorned with stonework and a life-sized marble statue of Jones, who was a [dry goods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dry_goods "Dry goods") store owner in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"). This sculpture of Jones represents him in period costume.

The **Civil War Soldiers Monument** (1890)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-25) was erected in honor of the [Union Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Army "Union Army") veterans of the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), most of whom served in Company H of the [32nd New York Infantry Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32nd_New_York_Infantry_Regiment "32nd New York Infantry Regiment"). The Company was composed exclusively of local volunteers from the [Tarrytown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarrytown,_New_York "Tarrytown, New York") area. They fought in the [First Battle of Bull Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Battle_of_Bull_Run "First Battle of Bull Run"), the [Peninsular Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsular_Campaign "Peninsular Campaign"), and the Battles of [South Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_South_Mountain "Battle of South Mountain"), [Antietam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Antietam "Battle of Antietam"), and [Chancellorsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Chancellorsville "Battle of Chancellorsville"). Many of them are buried in the cemetery, near the monument. Its granite base is topped by a 7-foot-6-inch bronze statue of a Union infantry soldier standing at "parade rest"; bronze plaques on the base list some 240 names.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-26)

**John Hudson Hall Monument** (1894) is one of the most popular and visually striking monuments in the cemetery. Hall was a highly successful paper manufacturer, a developer of New York's elevated railroad system, and an [art patron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage "Patronage") who amassed a large personal collection and commissioned the famous sculptor [Augustus Saint-Gaudens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Saint-Gaudens "Augustus Saint-Gaudens") to create his funerary monument.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-27) It is a rare stone version of Saint-Gaudens' masterpiece, _Amor Caritas (Angel of Charity)_, his vision of the ethereal female, which he modeled repeatedly between 1880 and 1898. A heroic-sized (larger than life-size) bronze version won the Grand Prize at the Paris [Exposition Universelle of 1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Universelle_(1900) "Exposition Universelle (1900)"),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-28) cementing Saint-Gaudens' reputation as America's premier sculptor. Because of its popularity, some 20 smaller-scale versions were produced by Saint-Gaudens and sold through high-end retail outlets such as [Tiffany & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiffany_&_Co. "Tiffany & Co.")[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:02-29) Most of them are now in museums, including the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-30) The face of the angel is modeled after the artist's longtime mistress and muse, Davida Johnson Clark.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-31) In the Hall Memorial version, the angel is set into a massive granite [pedestal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedestal "Pedestal") featuring a [bas-relief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relief "Relief") portrait of Hall himself at the base.

**Revolutionary Soldiers' Monument** (1894)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-32) is a simple granite obelisk, but its location is significant: it was built on top of the cemetery's Battle Hill, which was a strategic local spot during the [Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"), where a [lunette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunette_(fortification) "Lunette (fortification)") (or [redoubt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redoubt "Redoubt")) had been built by American soldiers around 1779 by to guard a strategic [Albany Post Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany_Post_Road "Albany Post Road") crossing over Pocantico River.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:5-33) A Revolutionary War cannon is positioned in the same spot where a cannon was trained during the war to defend the crossing. Battle Hill may have been the place where [Hulda of Bohemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch_Church_of_Sleepy_Hollow#Hulda_of_Bohemia "Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow") (c.1700-c.1777), the semi-legendary "witch" of Sleepy Hollow, was killed by British soldiers while protecting the local militiamen.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:9-35) Funds for the monument were raised under the leadership of [Marcius D. Raymond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcius_D._Raymond "Marcius D. Raymond"), publisher of the local _Tarrytown Argus_ newspaper. It was erected specifically to honor the local veterans of the Revolution who are buried in the adjacent [Old Dutch Burying Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch_Church_of_Sleepy_Hollow#Old_Dutch_Burying_Ground "Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow"), which holds one of the highest concentrations of Revolutionary War veteran graves in the state of New York.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-36) The October 19, 1894, dedication was a major event: crowds from New York City and the area arrived by trains and excursion boats, a parade came up Broadway, and two Navy cruisers in the [Tappan Zee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tappan_Zee "Tappan Zee") provided a dramatic cannon salute.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-WFR-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-PALO-38) (Raymond later published a book detailing the celebration,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:0-23) which also contains invaluable historical data on related Revolutionary War events and the families whose names are inscribed on the monument.)

Not far from the Revolutionary Soldiers' Monument, on the very top of the Battle Hill, is another, much taller and significantly older monument–a granite pillar topped by a figure symbolizing Hope and surrounded by multiple marble figures. It is the **Delavan Monument**, dedicated in 1871 to the memory of General Daniel Delavan (1757–1835), who commanded one of the Westchester County Militia regiments during the War.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-39) The Sleepy Hollow Cemetery did not exist when General Delavan passed away; however, 35 years later, his son was able to move his father and several other family members from [Sparta Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarborough_Historic_District#Sparta_Cemetery "Scarborough Historic District") in Ossining to the Battle Hill, at which his father may have fought almost a century before.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-40) (The Delavan family was remarkably active in the war effort; family patriarch Timothy Delavan (1712–1803) and several of his sons, including Daniel, Samuel, and Nathaniel, are recorded as having served the American cause.)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-42)

**Edwin Lister Monument** (ca. 1898) is one of the most stunning memorials in the cemetery. The 12-foot-high structure was expertly crafted by the Connecticut company [New England Granite Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Granite_Works "New England Granite Works") and featured in the company catalog to showcase its skill in creating one-of-a-kind, custom memorials.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-43) Lister was a cofounder of Listers Agricultural Chemical Works, a massive fertilizer plant in [Newark, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark,_New_Jersey "Newark, New Jersey").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-44) Carved from gray granite, the monument features his stately bust atop a [sarcophagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus "Sarcophagus") flanked on either side by [Corinthian columns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinthian_order "Corinthian order"), supporting a [lintel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lintel "Lintel") and [cornice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornice "Cornice"). However, the most prominent feature of the monument is a life-sized, sorrowing female figure seated on its base, resting her head on her proper right hand[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-45)—a striking example of [Victorian-era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era "Victorian era") funerary sentiment.

**Recueillement**, also known as **Bronze Lady** (1903), is a mournful seated statue across from Gen. [Samuel Russell Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Russell_Thomas "Samuel Russell Thomas")'s mausoleum, commissioned by his widow, Ann Porter Thomas, from the noted sculptor [Andrew O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_O'Connor_(sculptor) "Andrew O'Connor (sculptor)"). Many visitors and experts have praised the statue's life-like appearance and the "enchanting" quality of the bronze work. Others, including Thomas's widow, have felt disturbed by the statue's haunted, unsettling expression. The widow asked O'Connor to replace the statue's head; the sculptor, however, refused.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-46) The statue has become a centerpiece of local legendry.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-49) It is one of the most visited memorials in the cemetery.

**Henry Villard Memorial** (1904) was designed by the prominent architectural sculptor [Karl Bitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Bitter "Karl Bitter") for the gravesite of the journalist and financier [Henry Villard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Villard "Henry Villard"). It is a rare and notable example of the [Art Nouveau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Nouveau "Art Nouveau") movement in American cemetery sculpture and in American [funerary art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funerary_art "Funerary art") in general. The central life-size marble figure, titled "Labor at Rest," depicts a man resting against an anvil while holding a sledgehammer. This imagery reflects Villard's career as a railroad tycoon.

**John Dustin Archbold Mausoleum** (1906) is a notable example of Gilded Age [funerary architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funerary_art "Funerary art"). Due to its distinct [Byzantine-inspired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_architecture "Byzantine architecture")[dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dome "Dome") and other “Eastern” architectural elements, it contrasts with the cemetery’s other, more traditional [Neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") mausoleums. It features a one-of-a-kind green granite exterior and a spectacular glass mosaic ceiling inside, crafted by prominent [stained-glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass "Stained glass") designer Otto Heinigke,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-50) depicting Christian symbols and angels.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:4-51) The structure, built by the prominent construction firm the [Norcross Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norcross_Brothers "Norcross Brothers"), measures 36 feet by 36 feet and is 32 feet tall; it contains 12 crypts.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:4-51) The design for the mausoleum was commissioned by [John Dustin Archbold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dustin_Archbold "John Dustin Archbold") himself from the New York firm of [Morris, Butler & Rodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Wistar_Morris_(architect) "Benjamin Wistar Morris (architect)");[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:4-51) it was published in the _American Architect and Building News_ in 1906. Before Archbold’s own death in 1916, it notably served as a temporary resting place for [Laura Spelman Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Spelman_Rockefeller "Laura Spelman Rockefeller"), wife of [John D. Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_D._Rockefeller "John D. Rockefeller"), for four and a half months, due to legal and tax complications delaying her final burial in Cleveland, Ohio.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:4-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-52) The Archbold Mausoleum is situated directly across from the William Rockefeller Mausoleum.

**William Rockefeller Mausoleum** (1920) was designed by architect [William Welles Bosworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_W._Bosworth "William W. Bosworth"), who later restored the [Palace of Versailles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Versailles "Palace of Versailles"), for the family of [William Rockefeller Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Rockefeller_Jr. "William Rockefeller Jr.") Rockefeller commissioned the building after his wife of 56 years, Almira Geraldine Goodsell Rockefeller, died.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-1935Burial-53) Its construction was a major local event; in 1922, _The New York Times_ reported on the difficulty of moving a 32-ton block of granite (for the mausoleum's unique single-slab walkway) to the site.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-54) The [Neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") tomb, with [Ionic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_order "Ionic order") columns and a pyramid-style roof, is over 35 feet across, more than 43 feet deep, and 38 feet 5 inches high.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-55) Rockefeller bypassed the customary bold, high-profile placement of the family name above the entrance, opting instead for a subtle inscription on the bottom step of the [stylobate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylobate "Stylobate"). The mausoleum is situated on a hilltop plot[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:3-7) called Rockefeller Circle, less than a mile south of his (since demolished) extensive estate, [Rockwood Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockwood_Hall "Rockwood Hall"), where he resided for 36 years and where he died. One of his sons, [William Goodsell Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Goodsell_Rockefeller "William Goodsell Rockefeller"), is buried alongside his parents in the mausoleum vault.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-1935Burial-53)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-56) Other descendants, including son [Percy Avery Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Avery_Rockefeller "Percy Avery Rockefeller"), dauthter [Geraldine Rockefeller Dodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geraldine_Rockefeller_Dodge "Geraldine Rockefeller Dodge"), and grandson [Marcellus Hartley Dodge Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcellus_Hartley_Dodge_Jr. "Marcellus Hartley Dodge Jr."), as well as Byron M. Hawks, the family's estate superintendent of many years,[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-57) are buried under uniform granite gravestones around the perimeter of the mausoleum.

**Andrew Carnegie's gravestone** (1923) was erected four years after his burial in the cemetery. In keeping with his wishes, it is intentionally simple, reflecting Carnegie's philosophy on wealth and philanthropy, expressed in his famous article "[The Gospel of Wealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gospel_of_Wealth "The Gospel of Wealth")." The granite slab for the headstone was hewn from a quarry on the [Skibo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skibo_Castle "Skibo Castle") estate in [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland"), Andrew Carnegie's home, and sent to sculptor [George Henry Paulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Henry_Paulin "George Henry Paulin") at his studio in [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow"), where it was sculpted into a [Celtic cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_cross "Celtic cross"),[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-58) before being shipped to the United States. Surrounding his grave are the final resting places of his loyal household staff, including his butler, nurse, and chambermaid, all of whom were also born in Scotland.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-59) It is common for visitors to leave coins on his gravestone as a tribute to his philanthropic legacy or for good fortune.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-60)

**Helmsley Mausoleum** (2005-2007), the final resting place of [Harry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Helmsley "Harry Helmsley") and [Leona Helmsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leona_Helmsley "Leona Helmsley"), features windows showing a stylized [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan") skyline in [stained glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass "Stained glass") that only includes buildings Harry Helmsley owned or controlled, such as the [Empire State Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_State_Building "Empire State Building"), once the centerpiece of the Helmsley real estate empire.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-61) The mausoleum was built by Mrs. Helmsley at a cost of $1.4 million. She had her husband's body moved from its original resting place in [Woodlawn Cemetery (Bronx, New York)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodlawn_Cemetery_(Bronx,_New_York) "Woodlawn Cemetery (Bronx, New York)") to the new mausoleum because a new, massive public mausoleum was built near their private plot at Woodlawn, spoiling the secluded, exclusive view she desired.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-dtm-62) She filed a $150 million lawsuit against Woodlawn Cemetery over the construction.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-63) The move to Sleepy Hollow Cemetery was not without controversy either: it was delayed when she cleared trees on the new property without obtaining proper permits, resulting in a temporary halt by village officials.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:6-64) Leona died two years after the new mausoleum was largely functional and Harry’s remains were moved there. The Helmsley sarcophagi, standing side by side on an inlaid marble floor in the center of the mausoleum, feature romantic inscriptions they wrote for each other.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:6-64)

The cemetery features numerous other memorials associated with stories—such as the Crane Monument erected by Gertrude Beekman,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-65) the grave of [Marcellus Hartley Dodge Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcellus_Hartley_Dodge_Jr. "Marcellus Hartley Dodge Jr.")[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-66) at the foot of the William Rockefeller Mausoleum, and the [murder–suicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder%E2%80%93suicide "Murder–suicide") story of the [Ford brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Webster_Ford "Malcolm Webster Ford"), purposely buried in the same grave.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-Slain1902-67)

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

Several outdoor scenes from the feature film _[House of Dark Shadows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House\_of\_Dark\_Shadows "House of Dark Shadows")_ (1970) were filmed at the cemetery's receiving vault. The cemetery also served as a location for the [Ramones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones "Ramones")' 1989 music video "[Pet Sematary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pet_Sematary_(song) "Pet Sematary (song)")".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-Ramone-73)

**Sleepy Hollow Cemetery** in [Sleepy Hollow, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow,_New_York "Sleepy Hollow, New York"), United States,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-4) is a non-profit, non-sectarian burying ground of about 90 acres (36 ha).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-SH-Famous-5) It is the [final resting place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemetery "Cemetery") of numerous famous figures, including [Washington Irving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Irving "Washington Irving"), who was a cofounder of the establishment. Incorporated in 1849 as Tarrytown Cemetery, it was renamed Sleepy Hollow Cemetery in 1865.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:1-6)

The cemetery is contiguous with, but separate from, the [Burial Ground of the](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch_Church_of_Sleepy_Hollow#Old_Dutch_Burying_Ground "Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow")[Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch_Church_of_Sleepy_Hollow "Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow"), which was a setting for Washington Irving's famous story, _[The Legend of Sleepy Hollow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Sleepy\_Hollow "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow")_. The [Rockefeller family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_family "Rockefeller family") estate, [Kykuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kykuit "Kykuit"), whose grounds abut Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, contains the private Rockefeller cemetery,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:3-7) which is located behind a high fence at the north end of Sleepy Hollow Cemetery.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:2-8)

Sleepy Hollow Cemetery was listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") in 2009.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-NRHP2009-2)

## History and design

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and design")]

In 1847, the [New York State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Legislature "New York State Legislature") passed the [Rural Cemetery Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_Cemetery_Act "Rural Cemetery Act"), which authorized commercial burial grounds in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). The law led to the burial of human remains becoming a commercial business for the first time, replacing the practice of burying the dead in churchyards or on private farmland. Almost immediately after that, a group of prominent local residents, headed by author Washington Irving and Capt. [Jacob Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirck_Storm#Jacob_Storm "Dirck Storm") initiated the building of a modern burial ground in the [Tarrytown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarrytown,_New_York "Tarrytown, New York") area,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-10) as the Burying Ground at the Old Dutch Church no longer had adequate burial space for the growing community.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-11) Tarrytown Cemetery was incorporated on October 29, 1849. On April 11, 1865, it would be officially renamed Sleepy Hollow Cemetery—the name on which Washington Irving had insisted from the beginning, but was initially overruled.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:1-6) The new cemetery began with 39 acres north of the church graveyard, subsequently growing by about 41 acres in 1886 and an additional 10 acres in 1890.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-12)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-size-1)

It was designed as a [garden—or rural—cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_cemetery "Rural cemetery"), a style that was popular in the United States and Europe during the mid-19th century. (Washington Irving was a strong proponent of the garden cemetery movement.) Jim Logan, superintendent of Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, writes on his website, _Sleepy Hollow Country_: "Think of it as the Victorian version of therapeutic landscape architecture—a place where grief could unfold amid natural beauty rather than urban gloom."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:1-6)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-13)

The building of this type of cemetery involved well-planned walkways and elaborately landscaped plantings of trees and shrubs.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-14) The Tarrytown/Sleepy Hollow area, with its rolling hills, old-growth trees, and the gently flowing [Pocantico River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocantico_River "Pocantico River"), was a perfect location for a garden cemetery. Before the widespread development of [public parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_park "Urban park"), Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, like other garden cemeteries, provided a place for the public to enjoy outdoor recreation in a park-like setting. In the 21st century, it is still a popular spot for locals to take a nature walk.

Names of prominent local families are found on stone-fronted family vaults built into the hillsides in the older section of the cemetery, but most of the burials are family plots with multiple tombstones. In the northern section, on the higher elevations, there are numerous mausoleums and large plots with elaborate monuments of "many New York achievers"[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-15) of the [Gilded Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilded_Age "Gilded Age").

The cemetery's historic **Hillside [Receiving Vault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiving_vault "Receiving vault")** provided essential "cold storage" before the advent of modern [steam shovels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_shovel "Steam shovel") and [backhoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backhoe "Backhoe"). Built directly into a steep hillside, the solid masonry structure used the earth's natural insulation to hold bodies when the ground was too frozen for burial. It is a contributing structure to the cemetery's 2009 listing on the National Register of Historic Places.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-16) The vault gained international fame as the crypt of Barnabas Collins in the 1970 film _[House of Dark Shadows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House\_of\_Dark\_Shadows "House of Dark Shadows")_. No longer used for mass winter storage, it is part of official cemetery tours.

**Purported "Headless Horseman" cemetery bridge.** A popular feature is the cemetery’s rustic bridge over a Pocantico River ravine, near a small waterfall and the river’s natural Cascade Pool. Cemetery superintendent Jim Logan writes: "Visitors have long associated it with the famous bridge from Irving’s tale, though it’s a much later addition to the landscape. Still, there’s something fitting about it—a wooden span over running water, framed by autumn foliage, that captures the atmosphere of Irving’s story even if it wasn’t part of his original inspiration."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:1-6)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-17)

## Notable monuments

The Irving family plot

The modest **[Washington Irving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Irving "Washington Irving")'s gravestone** (1859) is located in the Irving family plot, where his parents, brothers (including [Peter Irving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Irving "Peter Irving")), nephews, and nieces are also buried. According to his nephew and literary assistant, Pierre Munroe Irving, the author had selected the specific place next to his mother when visiting the cemetery several days before his death.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-18) Creating a unique literary landmark, the author is buried close to the historic [Burying Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch_Church_of_Sleepy_Hollow#Old_Dutch_Burying_Ground "Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow") of the [Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch_Church_of_Sleepy_Hollow "Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow"), where the graves of people who inspired _[The Legend of Sleepy Hollow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Sleepy\_Hollow "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow")_ characters are located.

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/WashingtonIrvingGrave.jpg/250px-WashingtonIrvingGrave.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WashingtonIrvingGrave.jpg)

Headstone of [Washington Irving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Irving "Washington Irving")

The 1926 gravestone index, _The Old Dutch Burying Ground of Sleepy Hollow,_ describes it as follows:[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:22-19)

> On the Northern edge of the burying ground, overlooking his beloved .... Hollow, rest the remains of the gentle Washington Irving: the shrine of thousands of pilgrims from the distant places of the earth. Marked by no tawdry memorial of elaborate sculpture, a simple marble slab indicates the grave; a slab ingeniously fashioned, with rounded comers and edges designed to foil souvenir collectors who have carried off piece-meal two earlier stones.

While earlier grave decorations in the Old Dutch Burying Ground were carved from [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone "Sandstone"), Irving’s gravestone was made from white [marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble "Marble"). It became the preferred material for [Neoclassical architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") and decoration of the post-Revolutionary period, chosen for its association with the purity and idealized forms of [ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_art "Ancient Greek art") and [Roman art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_art "Roman art"). Marble, however, proved to be a rather poor choice for exterior monuments: originally smooth and glistening, marble surfaces soften with time and become rough, grainy, and discolored.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-20) Also, like sandstone, marble is easy to chip. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it was a common, though destructive, practice for tourists to chip off small pieces of sandstone and marble grave markers of famous people as souvenirs.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-21) The Irving gravestone that people see today is the third iteration of the original grave marker; as mentioned above, souvenir hunters chipped away at previous ones, which eventually had to be replaced. (By the end of the 19th century, newly developed power tools would make it practicable to carve gravestones and monuments out of durable [granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-22))

Irving's gravestone is the most visited place in the cemetery. In the words of the [New York Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Supreme_Court "New York Supreme Court") justice [Isaac N. Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_N._Mills "Isaac N. Mills"):[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:0-23)

> Sleepy Hollow... The genius of Irving, whose remains, at his own request, rest within her soil, that sweet and gentle Father of American Literature, has made her name known and loved, as far and as widely as the English tongue is spoken.

**Darius Ogden Mills Mausoleum** (1883), designed by the famous architect [Richard Morris Hunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Morris_Hunt "Richard Morris Hunt"), was commissioned and built decades before [Darius Ogden Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darius_Ogden_Mills "Darius Ogden Mills")' death in 1910. Its construction coincided with the height of the [Gilded Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilded_Age "Gilded Age"), a period when wealthy industrial families built increasingly elaborate monuments in garden cemeteries such as Sleepy Hollow Cemetery. A [Roman temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_temple "Roman temple")-like structure with grand [Ionic columns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_order "Ionic order"), it reflects the [Neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") and [Beaux-Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaux-Arts_architecture "Beaux-Arts architecture") styles favored by the era's elite. Unlike many traditional mausoleums, it is noted for having large, floor-to-ceiling windows on each side and in the roof, designed to capture light and highlight the silver-painted stars on the walls and floors; it creates a play of light that symbolizes eternal life and celestial presence. Visitors can see the ornate [sarcophagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus "Sarcophagus") and interior decorations without entering, a rare feature in 19th-century funerary architecture.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-24)

The monument of Owen Jones (1884) is an example of [Gothic Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_Revival_decorative_arts "Gothic Revival decorative arts") architecture, adorned with stonework and a life-sized marble statue of Jones, who was a [dry goods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dry_goods "Dry goods") store owner in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"). This sculpture of Jones represents him in period costume.

The **Civil War Soldiers Monument** (1890)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-25) was erected in honor of the [Union Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Army "Union Army") veterans of the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), most of whom served in Company H of the [32nd New York Infantry Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32nd_New_York_Infantry_Regiment "32nd New York Infantry Regiment"). The Company was composed exclusively of local volunteers from the [Tarrytown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarrytown,_New_York "Tarrytown, New York") area. They fought in the [First Battle of Bull Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Battle_of_Bull_Run "First Battle of Bull Run"), the [Peninsular Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsular_Campaign "Peninsular Campaign"), and the Battles of [South Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_South_Mountain "Battle of South Mountain"), [Antietam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Antietam "Battle of Antietam"), and [Chancellorsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Chancellorsville "Battle of Chancellorsville"). Many of them are buried in the cemetery, near the monument. Its granite base is topped by a 7-foot-6-inch bronze statue of a Union infantry soldier standing at "parade rest"; bronze plaques on the base list some 240 names.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-26)

**John Hudson Hall Monument** (1894) is one of the most popular and visually striking monuments in the cemetery. Hall was a highly successful paper manufacturer, a developer of New York's elevated railroad system, and an [art patron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage "Patronage") who amassed a large personal collection and commissioned the famous sculptor [Augustus Saint-Gaudens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Saint-Gaudens "Augustus Saint-Gaudens") to create his funerary monument.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-27) It is a rare stone version of Saint-Gaudens' masterpiece, _Amor Caritas (Angel of Charity)_, his vision of the ethereal female, which he modeled repeatedly between 1880 and 1898. A heroic-sized (larger than life-size) bronze version won the Grand Prize at the Paris [Exposition Universelle of 1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposition_Universelle_(1900) "Exposition Universelle (1900)"),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-28) cementing Saint-Gaudens' reputation as America's premier sculptor. Because of its popularity, some 20 smaller-scale versions were produced by Saint-Gaudens and sold through high-end retail outlets such as [Tiffany & Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiffany_&_Co. "Tiffany & Co.")[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:02-29) Most of them are now in museums, including the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-30) The face of the angel is modeled after the artist's longtime mistress and muse, Davida Johnson Clark.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-31) In the Hall Memorial version, the angel is set into a massive granite [pedestal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedestal "Pedestal") featuring a [bas-relief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relief "Relief") portrait of Hall himself at the base.

**Revolutionary Soldiers' Monument** (1894)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-32) is a simple granite obelisk, but its location is significant: it was built on top of the cemetery's Battle Hill, which was a strategic local spot during the [Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"), where a [lunette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunette_(fortification) "Lunette (fortification)") (or [redoubt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redoubt "Redoubt")) had been built by American soldiers around 1779 by to guard a strategic [Albany Post Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany_Post_Road "Albany Post Road") crossing over Pocantico River.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:5-33) A Revolutionary War cannon is positioned in the same spot where a cannon was trained during the war to defend the crossing. Battle Hill may have been the place where [Hulda of Bohemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch_Church_of_Sleepy_Hollow#Hulda_of_Bohemia "Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow") (c.1700-c.1777), the semi-legendary "witch" of Sleepy Hollow, was killed by British soldiers while protecting the local militiamen.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:9-35) Funds for the monument were raised under the leadership of [Marcius D. Raymond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcius_D._Raymond "Marcius D. Raymond"), publisher of the local _Tarrytown Argus_ newspaper. It was erected specifically to honor the local veterans of the Revolution who are buried in the adjacent [Old Dutch Burying Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch_Church_of_Sleepy_Hollow#Old_Dutch_Burying_Ground "Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow"), which holds one of the highest concentrations of Revolutionary War veteran graves in the state of New York.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-36) The October 19, 1894, dedication was a major event: crowds from New York City and the area arrived by trains and excursion boats, a parade came up Broadway, and two Navy cruisers in the [Tappan Zee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tappan_Zee "Tappan Zee") provided a dramatic cannon salute.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-WFR-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-PALO-38) (Raymond later published a book detailing the celebration,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:0-23) which also contains invaluable historical data on related Revolutionary War events and the families whose names are inscribed on the monument.)

Not far from the Revolutionary Soldiers' Monument, on the very top of the Battle Hill, is another, much taller and significantly older monument–a granite pillar topped by a figure symbolizing Hope and surrounded by multiple marble figures. It is the **Delavan Monument**, dedicated in 1871 to the memory of General Daniel Delavan (1757–1835), who commanded one of the Westchester County Militia regiments during the War.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-39) The Sleepy Hollow Cemetery did not exist when General Delavan passed away; however, 35 years later, his son was able to move his father and several other family members from [Sparta Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarborough_Historic_District#Sparta_Cemetery "Scarborough Historic District") in Ossining to the Battle Hill, at which his father may have fought almost a century before.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-40) (The Delavan family was remarkably active in the war effort; family patriarch Timothy Delavan (1712–1803) and several of his sons, including Daniel, Samuel, and Nathaniel, are recorded as having served the American cause.)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-42)

**Edwin Lister Monument** (ca. 1898) is one of the most stunning memorials in the cemetery. The 12-foot-high structure was expertly crafted by the Connecticut company [New England Granite Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Granite_Works "New England Granite Works") and featured in the company catalog to showcase its skill in creating one-of-a-kind, custom memorials.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-43) Lister was a cofounder of Listers Agricultural Chemical Works, a massive fertilizer plant in [Newark, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newark,_New_Jersey "Newark, New Jersey").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-44) Carved from gray granite, the monument features his stately bust atop a [sarcophagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus "Sarcophagus") flanked on either side by [Corinthian columns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinthian_order "Corinthian order"), supporting a [lintel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lintel "Lintel") and [cornice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornice "Cornice"). However, the most prominent feature of the monument is a life-sized, sorrowing female figure seated on its base, resting her head on her proper right hand[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-45)—a striking example of [Victorian-era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era "Victorian era") funerary sentiment.

**Recueillement**, also known as **Bronze Lady** (1903), is a mournful seated statue across from Gen. [Samuel Russell Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Russell_Thomas "Samuel Russell Thomas")'s mausoleum, commissioned by his widow, Ann Porter Thomas, from the noted sculptor [Andrew O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_O'Connor_(sculptor) "Andrew O'Connor (sculptor)"). Many visitors and experts have praised the statue's life-like appearance and the "enchanting" quality of the bronze work. Others, including Thomas's widow, have felt disturbed by the statue's haunted, unsettling expression. The widow asked O'Connor to replace the statue's head; the sculptor, however, refused.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-46) The statue has become a centerpiece of local legendry.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-49) It is one of the most visited memorials in the cemetery.

**Henry Villard Memorial** (1904) was designed by the prominent architectural sculptor [Karl Bitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Bitter "Karl Bitter") for the gravesite of the journalist and financier [Henry Villard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Villard "Henry Villard"). It is a rare and notable example of the [Art Nouveau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Nouveau "Art Nouveau") movement in American cemetery sculpture and in American [funerary art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funerary_art "Funerary art") in general. The central life-size marble figure, titled "Labor at Rest," depicts a man resting against an anvil while holding a sledgehammer. This imagery reflects Villard's career as a railroad tycoon.

**John Dustin Archbold Mausoleum** (1906) is a notable example of Gilded Age [funerary architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funerary_art "Funerary art"). Due to its distinct [Byzantine-inspired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_architecture "Byzantine architecture")[dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dome "Dome") and other “Eastern” architectural elements, it contrasts with the cemetery’s other, more traditional [Neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") mausoleums. It features a one-of-a-kind green granite exterior and a spectacular glass mosaic ceiling inside, crafted by prominent [stained-glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass "Stained glass") designer Otto Heinigke,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-50) depicting Christian symbols and angels.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:4-51) The structure, built by the prominent construction firm the [Norcross Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norcross_Brothers "Norcross Brothers"), measures 36 feet by 36 feet and is 32 feet tall; it contains 12 crypts.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:4-51) The design for the mausoleum was commissioned by [John Dustin Archbold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dustin_Archbold "John Dustin Archbold") himself from the New York firm of [Morris, Butler & Rodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Wistar_Morris_(architect) "Benjamin Wistar Morris (architect)");[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:4-51) it was published in the _American Architect and Building News_ in 1906. Before Archbold’s own death in 1916, it notably served as a temporary resting place for [Laura Spelman Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Spelman_Rockefeller "Laura Spelman Rockefeller"), wife of [John D. Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_D._Rockefeller "John D. Rockefeller"), for four and a half months, due to legal and tax complications delaying her final burial in Cleveland, Ohio.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:4-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-52) The Archbold Mausoleum is situated directly across from the William Rockefeller Mausoleum.

**William Rockefeller Mausoleum** (1920) was designed by architect [William Welles Bosworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_W._Bosworth "William W. Bosworth"), who later restored the [Palace of Versailles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Versailles "Palace of Versailles"), for the family of [William Rockefeller Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Rockefeller_Jr. "William Rockefeller Jr.") Rockefeller commissioned the building after his wife of 56 years, Almira Geraldine Goodsell Rockefeller, died.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-1935Burial-53) Its construction was a major local event; in 1922, _The New York Times_ reported on the difficulty of moving a 32-ton block of granite (for the mausoleum's unique single-slab walkway) to the site.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-54) The [Neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") tomb, with [Ionic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_order "Ionic order") columns and a pyramid-style roof, is over 35 feet across, more than 43 feet deep, and 38 feet 5 inches high.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-55) Rockefeller bypassed the customary bold, high-profile placement of the family name above the entrance, opting instead for a subtle inscription on the bottom step of the [stylobate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylobate "Stylobate"). The mausoleum is situated on a hilltop plot[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:3-7) called Rockefeller Circle, less than a mile south of his (since demolished) extensive estate, [Rockwood Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockwood_Hall "Rockwood Hall"), where he resided for 36 years and where he died. One of his sons, [William Goodsell Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Goodsell_Rockefeller "William Goodsell Rockefeller"), is buried alongside his parents in the mausoleum vault.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-1935Burial-53)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-56) Other descendants, including son [Percy Avery Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Avery_Rockefeller "Percy Avery Rockefeller"), dauthter [Geraldine Rockefeller Dodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geraldine_Rockefeller_Dodge "Geraldine Rockefeller Dodge"), and grandson [Marcellus Hartley Dodge Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcellus_Hartley_Dodge_Jr. "Marcellus Hartley Dodge Jr."), as well as Byron M. Hawks, the family's estate superintendent of many years,[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-57) are buried under uniform granite gravestones around the perimeter of the mausoleum.

**Andrew Carnegie's gravestone** (1923) was erected four years after his burial in the cemetery. In keeping with his wishes, it is intentionally simple, reflecting Carnegie's philosophy on wealth and philanthropy, expressed in his famous article "[The Gospel of Wealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gospel_of_Wealth "The Gospel of Wealth")." The granite slab for the headstone was hewn from a quarry on the [Skibo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skibo_Castle "Skibo Castle") estate in [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland"), Andrew Carnegie's home, and sent to sculptor [George Henry Paulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Henry_Paulin "George Henry Paulin") at his studio in [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow"), where it was sculpted into a [Celtic cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_cross "Celtic cross"),[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-58) before being shipped to the United States. Surrounding his grave are the final resting places of his loyal household staff, including his butler, nurse, and chambermaid, all of whom were also born in Scotland.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-59) It is common for visitors to leave coins on his gravestone as a tribute to his philanthropic legacy or for good fortune.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-60)

**Helmsley Mausoleum** (2005-2007), the final resting place of [Harry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Helmsley "Harry Helmsley") and [Leona Helmsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leona_Helmsley "Leona Helmsley"), features windows showing a stylized [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan") skyline in [stained glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass "Stained glass") that only includes buildings Harry Helmsley owned or controlled, such as the [Empire State Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_State_Building "Empire State Building"), once the centerpiece of the Helmsley real estate empire.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-61) The mausoleum was built by Mrs. Helmsley at a cost of $1.4 million. She had her husband's body moved from its original resting place in [Woodlawn Cemetery (Bronx, New York)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodlawn_Cemetery_(Bronx,_New_York) "Woodlawn Cemetery (Bronx, New York)") to the new mausoleum because a new, massive public mausoleum was built near their private plot at Woodlawn, spoiling the secluded, exclusive view she desired.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-dtm-62) She filed a $150 million lawsuit against Woodlawn Cemetery over the construction.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-63) The move to Sleepy Hollow Cemetery was not without controversy either: it was delayed when she cleared trees on the new property without obtaining proper permits, resulting in a temporary halt by village officials.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:6-64) Leona died two years after the new mausoleum was largely functional and Harry’s remains were moved there. The Helmsley sarcophagi, standing side by side on an inlaid marble floor in the center of the mausoleum, feature romantic inscriptions they wrote for each other.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-:6-64)

The cemetery features numerous other memorials associated with stories—such as the Crane Monument erected by Gertrude Beekman,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-65) the grave of [Marcellus Hartley Dodge Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcellus_Hartley_Dodge_Jr. "Marcellus Hartley Dodge Jr.")[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-66) at the foot of the William Rockefeller Mausoleum, and the [murder–suicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder%E2%80%93suicide "Murder–suicide") story of the [Ford brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Webster_Ford "Malcolm Webster Ford"), purposely buried in the same grave.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-Slain1902-67)

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

Several outdoor scenes from the feature film _[House of Dark Shadows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House\_of\_Dark\_Shadows "House of Dark Shadows")_ (1970) were filmed at the cemetery's receiving vault. The cemetery also served as a location for the [Ramones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones "Ramones")' 1989 music video "[Pet Sematary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pet_Sematary_(song) "Pet Sematary (song)")".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleepy_Hollow_Cemetery#cite_note-Ramone-73)
